sens: Gray or white powdery residue left by fire after combustion
Symbol of mourning, repentance, and humility in penitential rites
G4700.detail:
1. Ash is what remains when something has burned: a fine gray powder. This is the concrete meaning of the word. In Hebrews 9:13, it refers to the "ashes of a heifer" used in the purification rituals of the Old Testament — these ashes came from a completely burned red heifer, and its residue was used to ritually cleanse those who had become unclean.
2. Ash also signifies an attitude of repentance and mourning. When someone wanted to show sincere sorrow or repentance before God, they would cover themselves with ash — it was a visible, humiliating gesture that said, "I humble myself, I acknowledge my fault." In Matthew 11:21 and Luke 10:13, Jesus says that Tyre and Sidon would have repented "in sackcloth and ashes" if they had seen his miracles: meaning they would have shown true, public, and bodily repentance by donning these signs of humiliation.
G4700.origine: The Greek word σποδός comes from an ancient root meaning something powdery or reduced to dust. In biblical Hebrew, אֵפֶר (épher) carries the same concrete and symbolic meaning. The Greek word retains the image of fine powder, but it also denotes — particularly in contexts of mourning or repentance — voluntary humiliation: to cover oneself with ash was literally to soil oneself, to become unclean or unpleasant to signify to God that one acknowledged their faults.
G4700.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament. In Hebrews 9:13, it refers to the Levitical practice of purification by the ashes of a red heifer — a rite that symbolically predisposed one to purification by the blood of Christ. In Matthew 11:21 and Luke 10:13 (two parallel passages), Jesus uses it to describe the acts of repentance that Tyre and Sidon would have performed: the "sackcloth and ashes" form a traditional expression of visible and sincere repentance. In all cases, ash evokes a radically visible change of attitude — a break with sin.
G4700.portee: For the Christian, the word reminds us that true repentance is not a mere internal thought, but a change that manifests itself. Ash also speaks of what we are without God — dust and nothingness — and of our need to humble ourselves. Finally, the reference to the ashes of the heifer in Hebrews invites us to see how the Old Testament foreshadowed the complete purification brought by Christ's sacrifice: from the unclean to the clean, from sin to forgiveness.

sens: action of sowing
time of sowing
sown grain, offspring
G4701.detail: 1. The word σπορά primarily refers to the action of sowing — the gesture of the farmer scattering seeds on the ground (cf. the image of the parable of the sower). 2. It can also refer to the season of sowing, the time when one sows. 3. Figuratively, it applies to seed in the sense of offspring or progeny: in 1 Peter 1:23, Peter uses this term to speak of the "incorruptible seed" by which we are regenerated, meaning the living word of God that begets us spiritually, like a seed that produces new life.
G4701.origine: The word σπορά comes from the verb σπείρω (speirô), "to sow." It originally designates the action and result of scattering seeds. The corresponding Hebrew word in the Greek Old Testament is זָרַע (zara'), which has the same meaning. The family of σπείρω also includes σπέρμα (sperma, "seed"), which often carries the sense of offspring or promised progeny in the Bible.
G4701.emploi: The word σπορά appears only once in the New Testament, in 1 Peter 1:23. Peter uses it in a context of spiritual regeneration: we have been "born again" not by a corruptible seed (perishable), but by an incorruptible seed — the living and enduring word of God. This image from the Greek New Testament draws on the common biblical imagery that likens the divine word to a fruitful seed capable of producing new life. The choice of this term rather than the simple σπέρμα (seed) perhaps emphasizes the dynamic action of the seed that germinates and produces.
G4701.portee: This image of the "incorruptible seed" enriches the Christian understanding of regeneration: just as a seed contains within it the power to produce a new plant, the word of God within us produces a new, eternal, and imperishable life. It is an invitation to recognize the living power of the word of God, not as a dead doctrine but as a generative reality that transforms the one who receives it.

sens: land sown with grains ready to be harvested
by metonymy: the grains themselves that grow there
G4702.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to a field where grains, particularly wheat, have been sown and are awaiting harvest. It is the cultivated land itself, prepared and filled with its crop. When the evangelist says that Jesus "went through the fields of wheat" (Matthew 12:1), he is talking about the sown land that one walks through.
2. By natural extension, the word is also used to refer to the ears and the wheat itself that grows in this field. This is by metonymy: the content is named by the container. The three accounts of the Sabbath (Matthew 12:1, Mark 2:23, Luke 6:1) speak of the same fields, but the emphasis is on the wheat that is harvested by plucking the ears.
G4702.origine: The word comes from the Greek σπείρω (to sow). σπόριμος literally means "that which is sown" or "that which is suitable for sowing." It is an adjective formed from the root of the verb to sow, just as in French "cereal" comes from the Latin serendus. The basic idea is thus that of land dedicated to the work of sowing.
G4702.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, in the three synoptic gospels, all recounting the same event: Jesus and his disciples passing through a wheat field on a Sabbath day. Matthew, Mark, and Luke all use σπόριμος to evoke this rural landscape. The context is that of the Sabbath: the disciples are hungry, they pluck ears of grain and eat them. This detail of hunger and the improvised meal shows that the wheat field is a place of ordinary life, not just a backdrop — it is in these fields that the poor could feed themselves along the way.
G4702.portee: This simple and concrete word anchors the Gospel in real life: Jesus and his disciples do not float above the world, but they walk in the fields, they are hungry, they eat wheat. It is a detail that humanizes the narrative and shows how Jesus fits into the ordinary existence of his people. It is also the setting for a teaching on the law of the Sabbath: Jesus provokes a religious controversy precisely by passing through these mundane fields.

sens: Grain that is sown in the ground to germinate and produce a harvest
Action of sowing, moment of sowing
Word of God or teaching brought to faith
Gift or charitable action whose fruits will return to the giver
G4703.detail:
1. The seed is primarily the physical grain that a farmer throws into the ground: it is this small seed that contains life and from which the harvest will arise (Mark 4:26-27). In the parable of the sower, Jesus describes how the seed falls in different places — along the path, on the rock, among thorns — and germinates or does not germinate according to the quality of the soil (Luke 8:5).
2. The word also refers to the moment and action of sowing, the season of sowing: it is the crucial period when the farmer entrusts his seed to the earth in hopes of the harvest.
3. Jesus uses the seed as an image of the Word of God: "The seed is the word of God" (Luke 8:11). Just as a seed must fall into good soil to grow and bear fruit, the Word must find a receptive heart to transform a life.
4. Paul employs the same language for gifts and almsgiving: the one who gives generously "sows" a seed of righteousness, and God will multiply its fruits (2 Corinthians 9:10). This conveys the idea that charity, like a seed, bears fruit that returns to the one who sows it.
G4703.origine: The word sporos comes from the verb "to sow" (speirô). In Hebrew, the word "zera" (זֶרַע), of which sporos is the Greek equivalent, means both "seed" and "descendant, offspring" — for a seed produces a lineage of harvests, just as a person produces descendants. This double meaning enriches biblical imagery: a seed produces fruit, a word produces change, a charitable action produces results.
G4703.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, mainly in Jesus' parables about the Kingdom of God. Mark 4:26-27 and Luke 8:5-11 recount the parable of the sower and the grain that grows on its own: these verses play on the concrete image of the seed to teach how the Word acts in the believer's heart. Paul in 2 Corinthians 9:10 transposes the image to the moral and spiritual realm: the "seed" of the generous is no longer a grain of wheat, but a gift of money or kindness, of which God will multiply the fruits. From one passage to another, the word remains rooted in agriculture but takes on an increasingly spiritual significance.
G4703.portee: The seed teaches the believer three essential truths. First, that the Word of God works in silence, like a seed that germinates without one knowing how — the Christian must trust in its invisible effectiveness. Next, that the result depends on the soil: a hardened, distracted heart or one choked by worries will reject the Word, while a well-prepared soul will receive it and bear much fruit. Finally, that generosity is a seed: the one who gives entrusts their gift to God, who will make it fruitful beyond all expectation.

sens: to rush, to go quickly
to act with zeal, with fervor
to dedicate one's efforts to something
G4704.detail:
1. To hurry is primarily to rush, to go quickly: Paul says to Timothy, "Come to me as soon as you can" (2 Timothy 4:9), and to Titus, "Make haste to come to me" (Titus 3:12) — it is the urgency of one who cannot wait.
2. But the word also means to act with zeal, with lively application: the Thessalonians experience "earnestly the intense desire" to see Paul (1 Thessalonians 2:17), which shows a fervor of heart, not just speed.
3. The meaning expands to imply dedicating one's efforts to something, giving it diligence. Being a Christian means "to strive to maintain the unity of the Spirit" (Ephesians 4:3), "to apply oneself to enter into that rest" of God (Hebrews 4:11), or "to be eager to make your calling sure" (2 Peter 1:10) — in other words, one must actively aim for holiness.
G4704.origine: The word comes from the Greek σπουδή (spoudḗ), which means "haste" or "zeal." It expresses the idea of moving with energy, either out of urgency or fervor. In the Greek of the Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb בָּהַל (bahal), which means "to be hurried, to be afraid, to be frightened" — but also "to hasten." The Greek word retains the idea of rapid and energetic movement, whether motivated by fear, urgency, or passion.
G4704.emploi: σπουδάζω appears 11 times in the New Testament, mainly in Paul's epistles. It is first used to express urgency: Paul asks his collaborators to come quickly (2 Timothy 4:9, 4:21; Titus 3:12). But it soon takes on a moral and spiritual significance: in Ephesians 4:3 and Hebrews 4:11, it describes the constant effort of the Christian to advance in faith, "to strive" or "to apply oneself." In 2 Peter 1:10 and 3:14, it refers to "making sure" one's calling or being "found blameless" — a moral diligence. The apostle commands the faithful to have a "zealous diligence" (2 Timothy 2:15) in studying the Word. The word thus oscillates between the concrete idea of hurrying and the spiritual idea of fully engaging.
G4704.portee: This word calls the Christian not to remain passive: faith is not an easy possession, but requires vigilance, constant application. To hurry is to recognize that the grace of God deserves one's full investment. It is also an invitation to obedience without delay: when the Spirit calls, the heart that loves the Lord does not hesitate.

sens: Eagerness, haste to do something
Fervor, diligence in action
Enthusiastic devotion to a cause
G4705.detail:
1. The word first denotes an eager haste, a promptness to act without delay. In 2 Corinthians 8:17, we see this movement: the brother in question rushes forward of his own accord, driven by an inner impulse.
2. From this haste arises the idea of zeal — a constant fervor, a diligence that manifests in action. The text of 2 Corinthians 8:22 shows a man whose "zeal has been proven on many occasions": it is a disposition of the heart that unfolds regularly.
3. This zeal then becomes a sincere devotion to a cause or to people. Here, it is the devotion towards the church, towards mutual aid. It is serving with all one's heart, not out of compulsion, but out of true attachment.
G4705.origine: The word comes from the Greek σπουδή (spoudé), which literally means "haste" or "eagerness." This root evokes the image of someone who hurries, who runs with fervor towards a goal. The word thus describes an acceleration of heart and action, a natural enthusiasm that drives one to give their best.
G4705.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both in the same letter, 2 Corinthians 8, where Paul speaks of the collection for the church in Jerusalem. In verse 17, he qualifies the eagerness of the brother who rises up of his own accord to help. In verse 22, he describes a man whose diligence has been manifested "on many occasions." Paul uses this word to express not a cold obedience, but a fervor that comes from within, a generosity that expresses itself spontaneously. The context shows that it is a valuable quality in the service of the church.
G4705.portee: This word reminds Christians that it is not simply about performing religious tasks, but doing so with fervor and generosity. True Christian service requires zeal — not a nervous or feigned activity, but a sincere devotion that springs from love for God and for one's brothers. This quality distinguishes those who serve wholeheartedly from those who merely fulfill their duty.

sens: With lively haste, a particular fervor
With sustained and vigilant attention
With an increased urgency compared to usual
G4708.detail:
1. The word describes an action carried out with a certain benevolent haste, a hurry that arises from the desire to do well. In Philippians 2:28, Paul sends Epaphroditus "with all the more eagerness": this is an urgency motivated by love and concern for the well-being of others.
2. It also means doing something with diligence and vigilance, without dragging or neglecting. The heart puts in energy, like someone who is active because the matter truly matters.
3. In the comparative sense ("more eagerness"), the word emphasizes an intensification: one does not just do what is necessary, but does it with a heightened urgency, an additional zeal that reflects the importance of the issue.
G4708.origine: The word comes from the Greek "spoudê," which means ardor, haste, eagerness. The adverb "spoudaiôs" is its simple form ("with eagerness"), and "spoudaioterôs" is its comparative form ("with even more eagerness"). The root evokes the idea of rushing, of acting with passion. It is a word found in the family of zeal and diligence in New Testament Greek.
G4708.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Philippians 2:28, where Paul uses it in the comparative form. It is a decisive moment: Epaphroditus, a collaborator and friend, has been ill, and the Philippians have learned of it. Paul therefore sends him back "with all the more eagerness" so that they may rejoice at seeing him again and that he himself may be reassured. The urgency here is not panic, but a benevolent diligence, a "hurrying" that expresses pastoral love.
G4708.portee: This word invites the Christian to act with urgency where love demands it, without dragging their feet. It reveals that being attentive to the well-being of others is not a passive luxury: it is an active eagerness. For Paul, sending Epaphroditus back quickly and announcing it "with eagerness" is an act of love. The reader understands that brotherly diligence has a profound spiritual significance.

sens: with eagerness and fervor, without slackening
with haste, urgency
G4709.detail: 1. The word describes an action carried out with zeal, firmness, and constant commitment. To act "earnestly" means to do so with all one's heart and without wavering. In Luke 7:4, the Jewish elders address Jesus with "earnest supplications" for him to heal the centurion's servant — they do not cease to insist, driven by urgency and the conviction that it is right. Similarly, in 2 Timothy 1:17, Onesiphorus seeks Paul "earnestly," meaning he puts all his energy and determination into finding him. 2. The word can also emphasize the urgency of movement, a hurried speed. In Titus 3:13, Paul requests that Zenas and Apollos be sent on their way "earnestly" — he wants them to not delay, to hurry in sending them off.
G4709.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective spoudaios, which literally means "eager, zealous." The root conveys the image of a soul in motion, stretched toward a goal. The adverb spoudaiōs carries this tension of ardor and commitment. In Hebrew, the Greek Old Testament sometimes translates it with terms close to zeal and vigilant attention.
G4709.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament. In Luke 7:4, it describes the elders' supplications: they are earnest, full of insistence. In 2 Timothy 1:17, it modifies Onesiphorus's search for Paul: it is a quest carried out with fervor. In Titus 3:13, Paul uses it to order that Zenas and Apollos be sent off without delay — here the idea of haste and eagerness in execution plays a greater role. Each time, the word emphasizes an action that does not tolerate indolence or lukewarmness.
G4709.portee: This word reminds the believer that prayer, the search for God, and obedience to His commands require a sincerity without calculation, a commitment of the whole being. It invites us not to do the Lord's work half-heartedly or out of routine, but with a whole heart — earnestly, as if our life depended on it.

sens: Speed, haste to do something
Fervor, active eagerness in an action or endeavor
Diligence, sustained application to fulfill a duty
Energetic devotion to a cause, a faith, a person
G4710.detail:
1. The primary sense is speed: when Herod's daughter goes to find the king after her dance, she does so with haste, "with eagerness" (Mark 6:25). It conveys the idea of rushing, moving quickly toward a goal.

2. However, the word takes on a moral hue: it is the active fervor one puts into a task. Paul asks the Romans to carry out their actions — giving, exhorting, showing mercy — "with zeal" (Romans 12:8). It is not a tranquil slowness, but an engaged energy.

3. This eagerness becomes a stable quality: diligence, constant application. When Paul exhorts the Hebrews to "show zeal" for the assurance of hope until the end (Hebrews 6:11), he speaks of active perseverance.

4. Finally, the word denotes passionate devotion: zeal for an ideal or a cause. The Corinthians must excel "in zeal in every respect" in the work of charity (2 Corinthians 8:7), and Jude urges his readers to "contend for the faith" with that same total commitment (Jude 1:3).
G4710.origine: The word comes from the verb σπεύδω (to hurry, to press). It first designates what is quick and pressed; then it has taken on a moral charge to signify the ardor, the energy of the heart. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew בָּהַל (bahàl), which means to be troubled, to hurry, to act with urgency. The word remains marked by this dynamic idea: zeal is never passive or indifferent.
G4710.emploi: The word appears twelve times in the New Testament, mostly in Paul and in the epistles. It first denotes a rapid physical attitude (Mark 6:25, Luke 1:39: to hurry, to go quickly), but this concrete sense represents only two uses. The other ten passages speak of zeal as a moral quality: it is ardor in service (Romans 12:8, Romans 12:11), eagerness to respond to a trial or to help (2 Corinthians 7:11, 2 Corinthians 8:16), excellence in a task (2 Corinthians 8:7-8), spiritual perseverance (Hebrews 6:11, 2 Peter 1:5), and finally, devotion to defend one's faith (Jude 1:3). The word thus summarizes a dynamic: moving from physical haste to the heart's energy that characterizes the engaged disciple.
G4710.portee: For the believer, this word invites action without lukewarmness. Biblical zeal is not sterile agitation, but energy put to the service of an ideal — to grow spiritually, to serve generously, to defend one's faith. It is an invitation not to put off until tomorrow what belongs to God today, and to do things wholeheartedly, not out of weak obligation. Zeal implies a deep conviction: one truly engages only for what one truly believes is important.

sens: Large flexible basket made of wicker or soft material, used to transport or store provisions
Spacious container capable of holding large quantities
Emergency or escape basket used to lower or escape from danger
G4711.detail:
1. The basket is a large flexible container, woven from wicker or soft material, used to transport and store food. At the meals of the multiplication of the loaves, Jesus instructs the disciples to gather the leftovers: "they took up seven baskets full of the fragments that remained" (Matthew 15:37). These baskets, large enough, allow for the gathering and carrying of substantial amounts of bread.
2. The basket more broadly refers to any ample and deep container capable of holding much. When the disciples ask Jesus how many baskets full of fragments were taken up after the feeding of the four thousand, they refer to the same basket (Mark 8:20) — a sizable basket, distinct from the smaller "kophinos" used on other occasions.
3. In a perilous situation, the basket becomes a survival tool: Paul's disciples lower him "through the wall, in a basket" to save him from his persecutors (Acts 9:25). It is a basket or net sturdy and large enough to contain a man and serve as a means of escape.
G4711.origine: The Greek word σπυρίς comes from a root meaning wicker or woven materials. It describes a flexible basket, different from κόφινος (kophinos), which is smaller and more rigid. The basket was a common utensil in Mediterranean daily life, used for transporting provisions and practical needs. The word appears exclusively in the Gospels and Acts, always to describe concrete situations of provision or rescue.
G4711.emploi: The word appears 5 times, exclusively in the Synoptic Gospels and Acts. In Matthew and Mark, the basket is systematically associated with the two accounts of the multiplication of the loaves: after the multiplication of the seven loaves for the four thousand, it is a basket (σπυρίς) that collects the leftovers, while in other contexts a different basket would be mentioned. This basket evokes abundance and divine blessing: it manifests how Jesus fully satisfies the crowds. In Acts, the unique usage (Acts 9:25) changes meaning: the basket becomes the unlikely instrument of a miraculous deliverance, allowing Paul to escape his enemies. It shifts from a symbol of generous provision to a symbol of divine protection.
G4711.portee: The basket reminds us that God generously provides for the needs of His children — the leftovers that fill it testify to an abundance that exceeds demand. For Paul lowered in a basket, it illustrates how God uses the most humble and unexpected means to save His servants. This word invites the Christian reader to recognize divine providence in the ordinary and extraordinary circumstances of life.

sens: Unit of length equal to about 185 meters
Distance covered in a foot race
Track or course where an athletic competition takes place
G4712.detail:
1. The stadium is an ancient unit of length: 600 Greek feet, or about 185 meters or one-eighth of a Roman mile. The Bible uses it to measure concrete distances: Luke 24:13 speaks of the village of Emmaus "which was sixty stadia from Jerusalem" (about 11 kilometers), and John 6:19 describes the disciples who had "rowed about twenty-five or thirty stadia."
2. The stadium is also the length of an athletic race, as it corresponded exactly to the distance covered during the Olympic games. In 1 Corinthians 9:24, Paul uses this sporting context: "Do you not know that those who run in a race all run, but one receives the prize," inviting believers to strive for the Christian victory like athletes.
3. By extension, the stadium refers to the place itself, the track or arena where athletes compete — an image that Paul extends in his metaphor of the Christian life as a race.
G4712.origine: The Greek word stadion comes from a root meaning "to stand" or "fixed position." Originally, the stadium was the distance an athlete could cover without interruption: it became the standard unit of ancient races and by extension a universally used measure of length. The Hebrew word kippah (in some contexts of distance) does not exactly cover this Greek measure, as the Hebrews did not have this unified measurement system.
G4712.emploi: The word stadios appears seven times in the New Testament, notably in Luke and John. Luke uses it to specify geographical distances: Emmaus (24:13), the distance from Bethany (John 11:18). John mentions it in the context of the Sea of Tiberias, where the boat had traveled 25 to 30 stadia (6:19). Paul uses it only once, but decisively, in the metaphorical context of the spiritual race (1 Corinthians 9:24). Revelation uses it to describe cosmic distances: 1,600 stadia of blood (14:20) and the measurements of the heavenly Jerusalem (21:16). The term remains technical, precise, and unambiguous: it is always a measure.
G4712.portee: The stadium in the New Testament opens two perspectives. First, it reminds us that the Gospel is situated in a concrete, measured world, where distances and spaces matter — God incarnates in tangible history. Secondly, through Paul's race, it invites us to see our life of faith as an engaged athletic race: we do not run in vain, but to receive the prize of victory in Christ. This image gives the Christian life its dynamic character and stakes.

sens: Container made of clay, generally round and closed
Container intended to hold or transport liquids or precious substances
G4713.detail:
1. A vessel is a container shaped from clay and fired in a kiln, of which many can be found in the East. Originally, the word specifically refers to a jar for storing wine or manna, but it is used for any container of this type, regardless of its use.
2. In the Bible, the vessel serves to preserve what is precious or sacred: in Hebrews 9:4, the golden vessel contained the manna — the miraculous food that God had given to Israel in the desert. It is an object of protection and memory.
G4713.origine: The Greek word στάμνος comes from a root that evokes storage and preservation. The translators of the Greek Old Testament used it for several Hebrew words designating jars or containers: צִנְצֶנֶת (a closed jar) in Exodus 16:33, and בַּקְבֻּק (a flask or jar) in the Kings. It is a concrete word, without particular theological connotation.
G4713.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Hebrews 9:4. In this passage, the author describes the contents of the Ark of the Covenant at the time of the first covenant: he mentions the golden vessel that contained the manna. It is a very specialized term, used to speak of objects of worship and the tabernacle. In Exodus 16:33, the vessel that contained the manna was intended to preserve a portion for future generations, as a testimony of divine providence.
G4713.portee: The vessel that contained the manna reminds us that God preserves the signs of His faithfulness. The manna kept in this vessel was a material proof of the miracle and God's love for His people. For the believer, this vessel evokes the importance of preserving the memory of God's works and passing them on to future generations.

sens: Action of standing up, taking a position
Revolt, uprising against authority
Quarrel, dispute between individuals or groups
G4714.detail:
1. In its most fundamental sense, this word denotes the action of standing, of rising up. Therefore, it can mean a "position" or a "rank" that someone occupies. Hebrews 9:8 uses it in this primary sense when it speaks of the "rank" or access to the tabernacle.
2. The word takes on a political and military hue when it designates an insurrection, a revolt against established power. This is the sense in the accounts of Barabbas (Mark 15:7, Luke 23:19, 25): this man participated in a rebellion against Rome that was accompanied by murder. In Ephesus too (Acts 19:40), there is fear that an agitated crowd may be accused of "sedition."
3. From political revolt to interpersonal conflict, the word can designate a quarrel, a dispute that divides a group. In Jerusalem (Acts 15:2), Paul and Barnabas are at the heart of a heated "discussion" about circumcision; in the Sanhedrin (Acts 23:7, 10), a "discussion" arises between Pharisees and Sadducees, dividing the assembly.
G4714.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "histêmi" (ἵστημι), which means "to stand" or "to rise up." Stasis primarily denotes the action of standing or the position one occupies. By the time of the New Testament, it had taken on the meaning of "rebellion" or "quarrel": one who "stands up" against authority is a rebel. In Hebrew, the word it most often translates is "amad" (עָמַד), "to stand," which confirms this basic image.
G4714.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the New Testament, mostly in Acts and by Luke. It has two main uses: first, a political and military revolt. Barabbas is imprisoned for a "sedition" accompanied by murder (Mark 15:7, Luke 23:19, 25); the apostles fear that a riot in Ephesus may be attributed to Christians as a "sedition" (Acts 19:40); Paul is accused of having stirred up "seditions" among the Jews (Acts 24:5). Secondly, the word designates a quarrel, a division within a group: a heated "discussion" pits Paul and Barnabas against the Judaizers (Acts 15:2); in the Sanhedrin, the question of resurrection provokes a "discussion" that divides Pharisees and Sadducees (Acts 23:7, 10). The political usage predominates, but the word can denote anything that "stands up" or divides.
G4714.portee: This word reminds us that division and rebellion are realities that the Church and society have always faced. It also shows that the early Christians had to navigate between faithfulness to Jesus and the risk of being confused with the seditious movements of their time, a tension that readers of the New Testament are well aware of.

sens: Greek coin of significant value, equivalent to four drachmas
Weight used as a standard of measure
G4715.detail:
1. The stater is a high-value silver Greek coin: it is worth four drachmas, or about the wage of four days of work. Thus, it is a significant sum. In Matthew 17:27, Jesus asks Peter to find it in the mouth of a fish to pay the Temple tax for two people: this detail shows that the stater was sufficient to cover this mandatory tax.
2. Originally, the word designated a standard weight used to weigh precious metals and verify the value of coins. This metallurgical sense has remained in the background of the monetary sense: the coin was named as such because it represented a standard weight of precious metal.
G4715.origine: The Greek word stater comes from a root meaning "to weigh" or "to stand up" (the idea of a weight that stands in balance on the scale). It translates the Hebrew mishqal, which literally means "weight" or "that which is weighed." The stater was a well-known unit of account and weight in the Mediterranean world, particularly in Egypt and Asia Minor.
G4715.emploi: The stater appears only once in the New Testament, in Matthew 17:27. It is Jesus who speaks of it: he instructs Peter to go to the sea, cast a hook, and open the mouth of the first fish caught, where Peter will find a stater. This coin will be used to pay the Temple tax for two people. This context shows that the stater is a concrete, recognized, and used currency in Judea in the first century, even though it is a Greek coin. The miracle underscores Jesus' authority over all creation, even in material details.
G4715.portee: This passage reminds us that Jesus, although he is the Son of God, voluntarily submits to the civil and religious obligations of his people. He pays the Temple tax, not because he was obligated, but out of respect for the established order and to avoid "scandalizing" his disciples. It is a lesson in wisdom and freedom: the believer can respect the laws without being enslaved by them.

sens: Upright stake, post
Instrument of Roman execution where condemned individuals were nailed
The cross on which Jesus was crucified
The event of Jesus' death on the cross, or its redemptive significance
The suffering and renunciation that a disciple of Jesus must accept
The Christian message of salvation centered on the cross
G4716.detail:
1. In its literal and primary sense, a stake or post erected vertically. In ancient Greece, it was a simple instrument before becoming the most infamous Roman execution method.
2. The Roman cross on which condemned individuals were executed. The instrument itself: "Jesus, carrying his cross, came to the place called the Skull" (John 19:17).
3. The specific cross on which Jesus was executed. The Gospels refer to it in the Passion narrative: "If he is the King of Israel, let him come down from the cross" (Matthew 27:42).
4. By extension, the death of Jesus on the cross, or its redemptive value for our salvation. Paul writes: "the message of the cross is foolishness to those who are perishing" (1 Corinthians 1:18), designating the entire thought of salvation in Christ.
5. In a figurative sense, the suffering and self-denial that each disciple must accept to follow Jesus. "Whoever does not take up his cross and follow me is not worthy of me" (Matthew 10:38) means accepting the sacrifices that the Christian life demands.
6. The teaching of salvation through the cross, which constitutes the heart of the Gospel. "Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ" (Galatians 6:14) summarizes the entire faith.
G4716.origine: The Greek word σταυρός comes from an ancient root meaning a stake or a palisade. In classical times, it simply meant a post or wooden barrier. It is only in later authors (Diodorus, Plutarch) that it designates the Roman instrument of execution. For the early Christians, the word thus carried a new and radical charge: an instrument of shame became the symbol of salvation.
G4716.emploi: The word appears 28 times in the New Testament. The four Gospels use it mostly in the literal sense, in the Passion narrative: Jesus carries his cross, is crucified on it, dies on it. Paul transforms the meaning by infusing it with theological significance: the cross becomes the central event of salvation (1 Corinthians 1:17-18), the means by which God reconciles the world (Colossians 1:20) and cancels our guilt (Colossians 2:14). The Synoptic Gospels also use the word in a figurative sense: taking up one's cross means accepting suffering and renunciation (Matthew 10:38, Mark 8:34, Luke 9:23). In Paul, the cross sometimes becomes synonymous with the death of Christ or the Christian message itself.
G4716.portee: For the believer, the cross is much more than an object or a historical fact: it is the heart of salvation and Christian identity. It reminds us that God acted to free us at the cost of the ultimate sacrifice. But it is also a personal call: following Jesus requires self-denial, acceptance of suffering, and contradiction from the world. Finally, it is the reason for our glory: not our own achievements, but the love of Christ manifested on the cross.

sens: to attach to a cross to cause death
to execute by crucifixion, a Roman punishment reserved for criminals
to make someone suffer by tormenting them
to radically renounce oneself or one's desires
G4717.detail:
1. The verb literally describes the action of attaching a person to a wooden cross to execute them: it is the punishment that the Romans inflict on the condemned, runaway slaves, and the worst criminals. Matthew 27:35 reports how the soldiers crucify Jesus and divide his garments at the foot of the cross.
2. This punishment causes a slow and agonizing death by asphyxiation and exhaustion: the verb thus designates this judicial execution. Luke 24:7 announces that the Son of Man "must be crucified," emphasizing the deliberate and foreseen nature of Jesus' punishment.
3. Figuratively, the word also describes moral torment and inner rupture: to endure the crucifixion of Jesus is to share in his suffering. John 19:20 mentions the place where Jesus was crucified, which has become a memorable site marked by this act of violence.
4. Galatians 5:24 and 6:14 use the verb in a spiritual sense: the Christian crucifies his fleshly desires and the world to live entirely for Christ, renouncing everything that separated him from Him.
G4717.origine: The verb σταυρόω comes from σταυρός (stauros), which first means "stake, palisade," then "cross." In ancient Greek, it was first said that stakes were driven in to build a palisade. The Romans adapted this word to designate their instrument of punishment: the cross. The Latin verb cruciāre (to torture) and the French crucifier also derive from it. This word was once rare among Greek writers, but it became common in the New Testament, as the punishment was well known in the first-century Roman world.
G4717.emploi: The verb appears 45 times in the New Testament. The four Gospels primarily use it to recount the Passion of Jesus: the Roman soldiers crucify him according to the prophecies and the order of Governor Pilate (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John). Paul also uses the word historically: the Jewish leaders and the pagans crucified the Lord (Acts 2:36, 4:10). Then, Paul uses the verb spiritually to exhort Christians: in 1 Corinthians 2:2, he asserts that he preaches "Christ crucified," the heart of the Gospel. In Galatians 5:24 and 6:14, he speaks of crucifying the fleshly passions and the world, meaning to radically renounce them. The word thus encompasses both the historical event and its spiritual significance for the believer.
G4717.portee: For the Christian, this verb concentrates the heart of the faith: Jesus Christ delivered to death on a cross. It is not just an infamous punishment; it is the means by which Christ bears the sin of the world and opens the way for reconciliation with God. Meditating on the crucifixion of Jesus calls the Christian to deep gratitude and a break with their own sinful desires: "I am crucified with Christ," Paul writes (Galatians 2:20 implicitly). The word invites contemplation of both the divine sacrifice and the renunciation it demands from its disciples.

sens: Bunch of ripe grapes, fruit of the vine
Image of the good or bad fruit that a tree or person produces
Figure of divine judgment and eschatological harvest
G4718.detail:
1. The word first designates, concretely, the bunch of ripe grapes — the tasty fruit borne by the vine. It is the ripe and edible product, unlike green or immature grapes. In Revelation 14:18, the "grapes of the earth" are harvested, an image of the final harvest.

2. In Jesus' teaching (Matthew 7:16 and Luke 6:44), the grape becomes a living parable: grapes are not gathered from thorns or brambles, just as figs are not picked from thistles. It is a moral lesson: from the good tree comes good fruit, from the bad tree comes bad fruit. The grape symbolizes the visible result, what reveals the deep nature of the person.

3. In Revelation 14:18, the image rises to an eschatological dimension: the ripe "grapes" of the earth are harvested for judgment, just as the ripe grain must be harvested. It is the classic biblical image of the divine harvest, where the ripe product is separated and judged.
G4718.origine: The Greek word σταφυλή translates the Hebrew עֵנָב (énav, "grape"). The root is ancient and common in Greek. The word specifically describes the bunch of ripe grapes, distinct from the word βότρυς (botrus) which refers more to the bunch on its branch or its less ripe state. The image comes directly from the Mediterranean agricultural world, where the vine and its fruits are constant metaphors for life, fertility, and divine judgment.
G4718.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament. It is first used literally in Matthew 7:16 and Luke 6:44, in the same teaching of Jesus about knowing trees by their fruits — a parallel passage in the first two Gospels. These verses pose a rhetorical question: who gathers grapes from a thorn? Answer: no one, for the nature of the tree determines its fruit. The third use, in Revelation 14:18, leaves the realm of moral judgment to enter the eschatological vision: the grapes of the earth are ripe and ready to be harvested by the angel, a prophetic image of final judgment. In all three cases, the word retains its symbolic and concrete charge.
G4718.portee: For the believer, this word recalls Jesus' saying: you know the tree by its fruits. Our lives produce fruits that reveal our hearts. It is a call to spiritual authenticity: not to settle for an appearance or a profession of faith, but to truly produce the fruit of the Spirit. In Revelation, the image of ripe grapes also reminds us that the time of judgment is coming, that history is not without end, and that the divine harvest will be fulfilled.

sens: The upper part of the stalk of wheat or a cereal, which bears the grains
By extension, the seed or grain itself borne by this stalk
G4719.detail:
1. The ear is the visible part at the top of the stalk of wheat or barley, the one that bears the cereal grains. It is the very image of the harvest: in Mark 4:28, the evangelist describes the growth of the grain — "first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear" — to show how the kingdom of God develops gradually, like a plant that matures progressively.
2. By metonymy (the name of the part for the whole), "ear" also designates the grain or seed itself that is harvested. When the disciples pluck ears in the fields to eat (Matthew 12:1, Luke 6:1), they are removing the wheat seed by rubbing it in their hands, thus transforming the ear into food.
G4719.origine: The Greek word στάχυς comes from an Indo-European root that designates what stands up, what is pointed, in accordance with the natural image of the ear that rises and stands above the stalk. In Hebrew, the word שִׁבֹּל (shabbôl) — often translated by the same word στάχυς in the Greek Old Testament — literally means the flowering or the flowering part, revealing how the ear is perceived as the peak of the plant's development.
G4719.emploi: The word appears four times in the Gospels, always in agricultural and harvest contexts. Mark and Luke mention it during Jesus' passage through the wheat fields on a Sabbath day (Mark 2:23, Luke 6:1), while Matthew describes the same scene (Matthew 12:1): the hungry disciples pluck and eat the ears. Mark 4:28 is unique: it uses "ear" in the sense of a stage of growth, not to describe an action, but to illustrate the process of the development of the kingdom of God. In all these passages, the ear represents the richness of the harvest, the fruit of the farmer's labor.
G4719.portee: The ear reminds us that God provides for our material needs through work and nature. When Jesus allows his disciples to eat in the fields, he affirms that compassion for the hungry takes precedence over strict observance of rules. In Mark 4:28, the image of the growing ear teaches Christians patience and trust: the Kingdom unfolds according to God's timing, not according to our impatience.

sens: Christian man mentioned in Paul's letter to the Romans
G4720.detail: Stachys is a Christian whom Paul personally greets at the end of his letter to the Romans. Paul calls him his "beloved," indicating that they had a personal and affectionate relationship. He lived in Rome and was a member of the Christian assembly in the city at the time Paul was writing this letter.
G4720.origine: The name Stachys, of Greek origin, literally means "ears" (like ears of wheat). It is a meaningful name that evokes harvest or fertility, common among Greeks of that time. The name appears only once in the New Testament.
G4720.emploi: Stachys is mentioned only once in the New Testament, in Romans 16:9, where Paul personally greets him. This unique mention occurs in the final section of the epistle, where the apostle addresses individual greetings to the Christians in Rome. This brief but affectionate mention reflects the importance Paul placed on personal relationships within the churches, even with believers he may not have known directly.

sens: The covering of a house, which protects it from rain and the sky
By extension, the house itself or the hospitality received there
G4721.detail:
1. The roof is the upper part of a house, the structure that covers and protects it. In the Gospel, the four friends of a paralytic lower him through an opening made in the roof to present him to Jesus (Mark 2:4), which shows that it is indeed a covering that provides access to the inside of the dwelling.
2. The word also designates, metaphorically, the house itself or the space of hospitality it represents. When the centurion says to Jesus, "I am not worthy that you should enter under my roof" (Matthew 8:8, Luke 7:6), he literally means his house, but he especially evokes the honor and hospitality that a man's dwelling represents: to receive someone under one's roof is to welcome them into one's home, offering protection and hospitality.
G4721.origine: The Greek word stegē comes from the verb stegō, which means "to cover" or "to protect." It designates the roof as an element of covering and protection. This Greek word translates in several places in the Greek Old Testament the Hebrew word mekassé (מְכַסֶּה), which has the same meaning of that which hides or covers. The root evokes the idea of covering, protecting against the elements.
G4721.emploi: The word appears only three times in the New Testament, and only in the Synoptic Gospels. It always refers either to the roof of a house in the concrete sense (Mark 2:4, where it is about uncovering it), or to the house itself in the context of the hospitality offered to Jesus (Matthew 8:8 and Luke 7:6). The centurion uses the expression "to enter under my roof" to mean "to come into my home"; thus, he expresses his unworthiness to receive Jesus. The word remains anchored in the material image of the building but takes on a social and spiritual significance of hospitality and dignity.
G4721.portee: This humble and concrete word reminds us that Jesus incarnated himself in ordinary living spaces: houses, roofs, the dwellings of men. It invites reflection on hospitality toward Jesus and others, and on the grace that allows us to receive him despite our unworthiness. The centurion, by recognizing that he does not deserve to receive Jesus under his roof, demonstrates a humility and faith that Jesus praises.

sens: To cover, protect by putting something under cover
To cover, hide, keep silent
To bear, tolerate without complaint
To endure, withstand without faltering in the face of a trial
G4722.detail:
1. The original meaning of the word is literal: to cover something to protect it, like covering a roof to defend it from rain. The image is that of a covering that shelters something.

2. From this notion of covering arises a figurative meaning: to cover also means to hide, to keep silent about something, not to reveal or disclose it. It is to keep silent about what could be said.

3. To bear something without complaint is in a way to cover it, to accept it without bringing it to light or protesting. Paul says in 1 Corinthians 9:12: "we have not used this right; rather, we endure all things so as not to hinder the Gospel" — he tolerates difficulties without using them as a reason to complain.

4. To endure in the face of a trial means to hold firm despite obstacles. In 1 Thessalonians 3:5, Paul fears that the Thessalonians may not be strong enough to stand firm against temptation; the word describes the ability to resist without breaking.
G4722.origine: The word comes from a root meaning to cover or protect (like the Latin tegere). In the Septuagint, its presence is rare (notably appearing in Wisdom 8:17). The basic image — to cover for protection — naturally extends to enduring: one "covers" a difficulty by accepting it without disclosing it, then tolerating it without faltering.
G4722.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, exclusively in Paul. In 1 Corinthians 9:12, it designates the ability to renounce a personal right so as not to hinder the Gospel — a voluntary endurance. In 1 Corinthians 13:7, at the heart of the hymn to love, it states that love "bears" or "covers" all, meaning it overlooks faults without making them known. In 1 Thessalonians 3:1 and 3:5, Paul speaks of the impatience of the apostles in the face of the tribulations of young converts, and of the ability to hold firm against seduction — here, to endure means to persist without wavering. The word always illustrates a form of moral strength: accepting limits, offenses, or sufferings without breaking.
G4722.portee: This word shows that Christian endurance is not a resigned passivity, but an active strength: to bear all — renunciations, offenses, trials — while keeping one's faith and love for Christ intact. This is particularly important in 1 Corinthians 13, where the love that endures all proves to be the very measure of spiritual maturity.

sens: Unable to conceive children, for a woman
Not producing fruit or results
Empty of meaning, unproductive
Figuratively: forsaken, without resources
G4723.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: a woman who cannot have children. Elizabeth, the mother of John the Baptist, was barren (Luke 1:7), a painful situation as it threatened family honor and inheritance in Jewish culture. This word carries no shame: it describes a biological reality that God can transform. Sarah herself, although advanced in age, was able to conceive by faith (Hebrews 11:11).

2. The word extends to anything that does not produce: breasts that do not nurse (Luke 23:29) do not fulfill their function. Jesus announces unfortunate days when barrenness will become a blessing, as the coming suffering will be great.

3. In a figurative sense, in Paul (Galatians 4:27), the "barren" woman is forsaken, without children, without visible resources. But God fills her with blessings: the Church, born of the promise and not of the flesh, produces more children than she who relied on carnal rights.
G4723.origine: The Greek στεῖρος (steiros) comes from the same root as the Hebrew עָקָר (aqar), which denotes both barrenness and uprooting (the one who has no attachments, no descendants). The Greek word regularly translates this Hebrew in the Greek Old Testament. The central image is the absence of fruit, descendants, fulfillment: something that should happen does not happen.
G4723.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, always related to the issue of descendants. In Luke, it is the condition of Elizabeth (1:7, 1:36) and a paradoxical blessing in the days of the Apocalypse (23:29). Paul uses it allegorically in Galatians 4:27 to express how God transforms the impossible condition into an abundance of grace: the barren woman becomes more fruitful than the one who had status and power. In Hebrews 11:11, Sarah overcomes barrenness by faith. The word shifts in meaning according to the context: from personal drama to theological symbol.
G4723.portee: This word reminds us that barrenness, whether physical or spiritual, is never a final condemnation for those who believe in God. Elizabeth and Sarah embody the promise that God honors faith despite apparent impossibility. For readers without children, it is a word of dignity and hope. Paul also uses it to show that the Church, born not of carnal strength but of the promise, can produce an abundance that natural strength could never generate. The word invites us to rely on divine power rather than visible resources.

sens: to withdraw, to stand at a distance
to avoid someone or something
to keep away from, to abstain
G4724.detail:
1. In the primary sense, it is the idea of retreating, standing away: when one "departs" from something or someone, distance is created. In 2 Thessalonians 3:6, Paul urges Christians to "depart" from every brother who lives in disorder — this is a call to fraternal separation, not to associate with his conduct.

2. The meaning then narrows to the idea of avoiding, keeping away. This can mean "not exposing oneself to" or "staying away from" something reprehensible. It is to preserve oneself from a situation, a person, or an influence.

3. In 2 Corinthians 8:20, Paul says that he and his companions "act" with caution in managing the gifts: here the word denotes vigilance, a circumspect conduct, an attention to not give rise to blame. It is less about "departing" than about "conducting oneself with restraint, with care".

4. The verb can also express abstention, deliberate refusal: one "departs" when one chooses not to do or approve something.
G4724.origine: The Greek word στέλλω comes from a root that evokes the idea of "regulating, arranging, putting in order". Originally, it meant "to place, to dispose" (as one prepares something); then it took on the meaning of "gathering, collecting" (as one rolls up a ship's sail), from which derives "to restrain, to control". In the passive or middle voice, it means "to hold back, to control oneself, to stay away". In the Greek Old Testament, it translates Hebrew verbs expressing respectful fear or the act of withdrawing (like חָתַת, "to tremble", in Malachi 2:5).
G4724.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, in the two provided usages. In 2 Corinthians 8:20, Paul uses it to express ethical caution in the administration of offerings: he himself "acts" with scruple to avoid any reproach. In 2 Thessalonians 3:6, it takes on a more directive sense: the Thessalonians must "depart" from those who live in disorder and disobey apostolic instructions. The word thus carries both a dimension of personal caution (not compromising oneself) and community discipline (separating from the wrongdoers).
G4724.portee: This word speaks to us of two closely related but distinct Christian attitudes: personal vigilance and fraternal separation. In 2 Corinthians, Paul teaches us to conduct our affairs with such clear honesty that it disarms even suspicions — it is a call to transparency. In 2 Thessalonians, he reminds us that the life of the Church sometimes involves a difficult act: standing apart from one who refuses to walk according to received principles, not out of contempt, but to preserve the order and holiness of the body.

sens: woven or braided ornament wrapped around a sacrificial victim
crown or garland woven
G4725.detail:
1. The ribbon is an ornament that is wrapped around an animal before it is sacrificed to the gods. It is a sign of respect and solemnity: the more adorned the offering, the more beautiful and precious the sacrifice. In Acts 14:13, the priest of Jupiter brings bulls adorned with ribbons, ready to offer them in sacrifice — for the inhabitants of Lystra, this was a proof of greatness and piety.
2. The word also refers to a crown or garland of intertwined flowers or leaves, the type of ornament worn around the head during festivals and religious ceremonies. It is an object of beauty and magnificence.
G4725.origine: The word comes from the verb στέφω (stephô), which means "to wrap around, to crown". The root evokes the idea of putting something in a circle, draping or encircling. The ribbon is thus literally what wraps and adorns. This type of object was common in Greco-Roman religion, where unadorned sacrifices would have had no value.
G4725.emploi: The word στέμμα appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 14:13. It is in the context where the inhabitants of Lystra, seeing the miracles of Paul, believe that the apostles are gods sent from heaven: the priest of Jupiter prepares a sacrifice by bringing bulls adorned with ribbons to honor Paul and Barnabas. The use of the word reveals the pagan religious context of the scene and shows how non-Christians glorified their deities. It is a detail that underscores the misunderstanding of the crowds: they desire to worship men.
G4725.portee: This word reminds us how, in a world without the Revelation of God, humans expend effort and wealth to honor false gods. It also shows that Paul rejected this worship only because he knew that only God deserves adoration. For the Christian reader, it is a lesson: the ornaments and magnificence of rituals mean nothing if they do not serve the true God.

sens: Cry or sound of pain, affliction
Muffled complaint expressing deep suffering
Silent prayer, intercession of the heart that transcends words
G4726.detail:
1. A groaning is a cry or sound of pain that comes from the mouth of someone who is suffering. In Acts 7:34, Moses reports that God heard the groanings of the oppressed people of Israel in Egypt — these plaintive complaints expressed the burden under Pharaoh's yoke.

2. More broadly, it is a muffled and deep complaint, a sigh that comes from the depths of the heart. Romans 8:26 speaks of "groanings too deep for words" by which the Holy Spirit intercedes for us: these groanings are not articulated words, but the expression of a pain so great that it transcends human language.

3. On a spiritual level, groaning becomes a silent prayer — an intercession of the heart. It is how our weakness manifests before God, and how the Holy Spirit helps us pray when our words fail.
G4726.origine: The word comes from the verb stenazô (stenázô), which means "to groan" or "to sigh." This root evokes the image of a person oppressed who cannot hold back their cry of pain. The word appears in the Greek Old Testament to translate several Hebrew words that denote cries of distress and complaints from the suffering people.
G4726.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Acts 7:34, it refers to the audible complaint of the people of Israel, a collective cry of oppression that God hears and that prompts Him to act. In Romans 8:26, Paul uses it to describe the silent sighs of the Holy Spirit in prayer: the emphasis shifts from the audible cry to the inner intercession, to the groanings that remain inexpressible in words. It is a tension between what is said and what is felt beyond words.
G4726.portee: For the Christian, this word reveals that God listens to and recognizes our suffering, even when it is too deep for words. It also assures us that the Holy Spirit intercedes for us, especially when we are weak and do not know how to pray as we ought. Our inner groanings — our cries of distress or heartaches — are never lost; they are carried before the throne of God by the Spirit Himself.

sens: To make a low, deep sound expressing suffering, pain, or emotion
To express internally, without speaking, a deep feeling of disappointment, regret, or fatigue
To murmur, complain against someone
G4727.detail:
1. To groan is primarily to let out a sigh or groan that expresses suffering or intense emotion: it is a sound that comes from deep within. When Jesus heals the deaf-mute in Mark 7:34, He "sighs" as He looks up to heaven — it is a sigh filled with compassion in the face of human misery.
2. The word also denotes a deep feeling that one keeps inside, which cannot really be expressed in words. This is what Paul describes in Romans 8:23: Christians "groan" within themselves, waiting for the day when God will transform their mortal bodies — it is a silent longing, a pain of the heart that one bears while awaiting final redemption.
3. In some cases, to groan takes on the meaning of murmuring or complaining: in James 5:9, "do not grumble against one another" — it is the expression of discontent that is often implied without being openly shouted.
G4727.origine: The word comes from a root that imitates the low and deep sound of groaning — it is an onomatopoeic word, like many words for sounds. In Hebrew and Aramaic, similar verbs meaning to groan or sigh (אָנַח, אָנַק) express the same sound of a body in distress. The family of the Greek word also includes compounds: "to groan together" (συν-στενάζω) reinforces this idea of shared suffering.
G4727.emploi: The verb appears six times in the New Testament. It first describes a concrete groaning or sigh: Jesus sighs in Mark 7:34 in response to human distress. Then it takes on a more internal meaning: Paul uses it twice in 2 Corinthians 5:2-4 to express how Christians groan in their mortal bodies, longing for eternal life — it is a silent suffering, a deep spiritual pain. In Romans 8:23, it is again this silent sigh of Christian hope. In Hebrews 13:17, spiritual leaders should not carry out their ministry with groaning or reluctance. Finally, in James 5:9, it takes on the meaning of murmuring or complaining among brothers. The word always expresses something restrained, internal — rarely an open cry, rather a sound that rises from within.
G4727.portee: For the Christian, this word reminds us that we are not alone in our suffering or longing for perfect life with God. Paul shows that to groan is also to wait — it is the silent cry of one who believes in resurrection and new life. But the word also warns: do not groan bitterly against others, for that is to live without trust in God. It is a word that speaks of the weight of the mortal body and the desire for transformation that God has placed in the hearts of His own.

sens: Having little width, confined in space
Figuratively: limited, restricted, requiring effort and renunciation
G4728.detail:
1. The word first describes what is physically narrow, confined — a narrow door, a narrow path, as opposed to something wide and spacious. It is the concrete image of the word.
2. In the New Testament, Jesus uses this word figuratively to speak of the door and the path that lead to eternal life. "Narrow is the gate, and difficult is the way that leads to life" (Matthew 7:14): Jesus tells us that following God requires renunciation, discipline, and effort — it is a difficult and narrow path, not a wide and easy road. Few people find it, for one must truly strive to enter (Luke 13:24).
G4728.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that means to tighten, to compress. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates צַר (tsar), which means narrow and oppressed. The word evokes the idea of something that presses, confines, or reduces space — like a mountain road wedged between two cliffs.
G4728.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, all in Jesus' teaching on the two paths. In Matthew 7:13-14, Jesus contrasts the narrow gate and the narrow way (which leads to life) with the wide gate and the broad way (which leads to destruction). This is a central teaching: the way of the Kingdom requires renunciation and steadfastness. In Luke 13:24, Jesus repeats this message urgently: "Strive to enter through the narrow gate," for many will seek to enter and will not be able — which suggests that the word "narrow" also implies difficulty, a moral and spiritual requirement.
G4728.portee: This word speaks to the heart of every believer. It reminds us that the Christian life is not a comfortable wide boulevard, but a narrow path that requires effort, sacrifice, and faithfulness. But this is not to discourage us: it is to lovingly warn us that we must truly commit, renounce sin and selfishness, and follow Jesus steadfastly. The contrast between the wide gate and the narrow gate urges us to examine our hearts: which path are we truly taking?

sens: To be compressed, crushed, pressed from all sides
To be lacking, to lack space or air
To be anxious, suffocated by anxiety or distress
To lack inner freedom, heart expansion
G4729.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to be compressed, pressed, like a person squeezed from all sides. It is the image of a narrow alley or a cage that constricts the body (cf. 2 Corinthians 4:8 "pressed in every way").
2. The word evokes a lack of space, narrowness: not having room to breathe, to move freely. That is why it also says "at the end" — cornered, with no escape.
3. In a figurative sense, it means anguish, emotional suffocation: being tightened by fear, pain, worry. Paul speaks of it as an inner sensation, an oppression of the soul.
4. More broadly, it is to lack openness of heart, generosity, hospitality. In 2 Corinthians 6:12, Paul tells the Corinthians "you are not restricted in us," which means he opens his heart wide to them, while they themselves remain closed, withdrawn into themselves.
G4729.origine: The Greek word combines two roots: στενός (narrow, tight) and χῶρος (space, place). This composition literally evokes "narrow space" or "to be in a narrow space." The verb thus describes the action of being reduced to tightness, pressed. The Old Testament speaks of similar situations with Hebrew verbs like צָרַר (to bind, to embrace) and אוּץ (to press), which also describe oppression, compression, distress.
G4729.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament, both times in Paul’s letters in 2 Corinthians (4:8 and 6:12). In 2 Corinthians 4:8, it refers to being "pressed in every way" — Paul describes the apostolic tribulations, persecution, and distress that constrict him. In 2 Corinthians 6:12, it concerns the opening of the heart: Paul tells the community that he opens his heart wide to them, while their "inward parts have been restricted" — this is the lack of generosity, moral and emotional narrowness. The word thus plays on both levels: physical/external and internal/moral.
G4729.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that external distress and oppression do not dominate hope (2 Corinthians 4:8), and that true liberation is a matter of an open heart. The apostle invites us to examine our soul: are we narrow, closed, withdrawn into ourselves, or do we open our hearts generously to God and others? It is an invitation to inner freedom, not to let fear or selfishness constrict us.

sens: Lack of space, physical narrowness
Feeling of oppression, suffocation
Moral or material difficulty, embarrassment
State of distress, spiritual tribulation
G4730.detail:
1. The word first paints a concrete image: narrowness, lack of space — one cannot move, one is squeezed, compressed. It is the image of someone suffocating in too small a space.
2. This image becomes sensation: anguish is that oppression felt in the heart, that tightening in the throat when fear or misfortune constrict us (Romans 8:35).
3. The word also designates the concrete difficulties that tighten life, embarrassment or calamity: Paul enumerates "tribulations, calamities, distresses" as the obstacles he faces as an apostle (2 Corinthians 6:4).
4. Lastly, anguish is the complete spiritual state of the heart under the weight of judgment or suffering — it is what God sends upon the sinner "tribulation and anguish" (Romans 2:9).
G4730.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that means narrow, tight: it is composed of elements evoking reduced space, suffocation. It translates the Hebrew צוֹק (tsuq), which has the same image of compressed space, crisis, or distress. It is a vivid and lively word: distress is not abstract, but corporeal — it is felt as pressure, a prison.
G4730.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, always in Paul’s letters (Romans 2:9; 8:35; 2 Corinthians 6:4; 12:10). It designates the sufferings of the Christian or the sinner: sometimes it accompanies tribulation as the weight of divine judgment (Romans 2:9), sometimes it enumerates the trials that the apostle endures for Christ (2 Corinthians 6:4; 12:10). Paul always places it alongside tribulation (θλίψις) with which it is closely related in meaning, but it adds the idea of internal oppression, suffocation of the heart. It is a word of lived suffering, not theoretical.
G4730.portee: This word reminds Christians that suffering is not just an abstract pain, but a reality that crushes, that oppresses — it is honest and concrete. But Paul also shows that these anguishes cannot separate us from Christ (Romans 8:35) and that they even become a place where His grace shines (2 Corinthians 12:10). Confessed anguish, named, becomes the door through which God manifests His strength.

sens: That is hard, compact, resistant
That is substantial, nourishing (referring to food)
That is stable, founded, unshakeable
That is unshakeable, constant (referring to faith or character)
G4731.detail:
1. The word first describes what is physically hard or compact, capable of resisting: it is the image of a dense and robust material.
2. In a more figurative sense, it applies to food: Hebrews 5:12 and 5:14 contrast "solid" food with milk, meaning a deep and nourishing teaching, intended to form spiritual maturity, as opposed to the elementary principles.
3. The word also expresses the solidity of a construction or an institution: in 2 Timothy 2:19, the "solid foundation of God" is unshakeable, established on truth.
4. Applied to faith or to the person themselves, it means moral firmness and constancy: in 1 Peter 5:9, a "firm" faith is one that holds strong in trial, without wavering.
G4731.origine: The Greek word στερεός comes from a root expressing hardness and solidity. It describes what is watertight, compact, incapable of being broken. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses related roots to express firmness and stability, particularly in architectural and moral images of an unshakeable foundation.
G4731.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, always in contexts that emphasize solidity or spiritual maturity. Two uses refer to spiritual food (Hebrews 5:12, 5:14): "solid" contrasts with "milk," meaning that deep Christian doctrine requires a mature heart. One use evokes the foundation of God (2 Timothy 2:19), unshakeable. The last speaks of firm faith in persecution (1 Peter 5:9). The word is always positive: it values what endures, what nourishes deeply, what stands firm.
G4731.portee: This word invites the Christian to progress toward spiritual maturity: not to remain on anything superficial, but to root oneself in a solid knowledge of God and His Word. It also reminds us that the Christian faith is not fragile or trembling, but founded on an unshakeable reality: that of the God who acknowledges His own. For those who suffer, it encourages a firm faith, not by human strength, but rooted in this very solidity of God.

sens: Make firm and solid, give solidity
Fortify someone, make them strong and capable
Affirm faith, make it unshakeable
G4732.detail:
1. The literal meaning is to make firm, solid, like wood or a construction that gains consistency. In Acts 3:7, we see this meaning applied to the feet of a lame man: his joints are "strengthened," becoming stable and able to support the weight of the body.
2. By extension, the word means to fortify someone, giving them physical or moral strength to act and progress. It is a reinforcement that touches the person in their entirety.
3. In a figurative and spiritual sense, to strengthen means to affirm faith, making it stable and unshakeable despite trials. In Acts 16:5, this is how the Churches "were strengthened in faith": their conviction in Christ became deeper and more solid day by day.
G4732.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective stereos (στερεός), which means "firm, hard, solid." The root evokes the idea of a compact and resistant material. This verb has an equivalent in Hebrew: the word raqaʿ (רָקַע) in Isaiah 42:5, which describes the stretching of the heavens, and hazaq (חָזַק) in Jeremiah 5:3, which expresses hardness or firmness. The word family includes terms that denote solidity, firmness, and immutability.
G4732.emploi: The verb stereoō appears only three times in the New Testament, all in the book of Acts. In Acts 3:16, it describes how faith in the name of Jesus strengthened the feet of a man lame from birth, giving him the ability to walk. In Acts 3:7, it is passive: the joints of this man are strengthened, solidified. In Acts 16:5, the word applies to the Christian community: the Churches as a whole are strengthened in faith, meaning their conviction becomes more robust and enduring. The context is always that of transformation or reinforcement brought by God, either physically or spiritually.
G4732.portee: This word reminds the believer that faith is not an ephemeral feeling, but something that must become solid and unshakeable. It shows how Jesus does not merely save: He heals bodies and strengthens the soul. For the Church, being strengthened in faith means growing together in a common conviction, in a stable and progressive manner, capable of withstanding the challenges of the world.

sens: physical solidity of a structure or support
strength, stability of a foundation or base
constancy and resolution in faith or convictions
G4733.detail: 1. The word στερέωμα primarily denotes a solid body, something stable and hardened that can support a structure — the image comes from a "solidified" or "strengthened" material. This is why the ancient Greek of the Septuagint uses it to translate the Hebrew firmament, that dome which the ancients believed was solid and which "supports" the sky (Genesis 1:6 in the Septuagint). 2. From there comes the foundational sense: a base, a support, that which gives something its structural stability. The image is concrete: like a rock or a column that does not move. 3. Finally, the word extends to moral and spiritual senses: the firmness of a position, the unshakeability of a conviction. Thus, in Colossians 2:5, Paul praises the "firmness" of the believers' faith — not a weak or wavering faith, but a solid and unshakeable adherence to Christ, like a base upon which all life rests.
G4733.origine: The word στερέωμα comes from the verb στερεόω ("to solidify," "to make firm"), built on the root meaning "hard," "solid." It is the same root found in στερεός ("firm," "solid"). In Hebrew, its most common equivalent is רָקִיעַ (raqîaʿ, "the extended sky"), literally "that which is extended or beaten" — for the sky was imagined as beaten and hardened like a metal sheet. The Greek word captures the idea of solidity and stability that characterizes the sky in the ancient biblical vision.
G4733.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Colossians 2:5, where Paul speaks of "the firmness of your faith in Christ." Here, "firmness" does not denote an abstract quality but a solid, unshakeable position: the faith of the Colossians holds firm, it does not waver under attacks or false doctrines (which Paul warns them about just after, in the following verses). The word evokes the stability of an architectural or geological structure — a faith "like a rock." Although rare in the New Testament, the word was common in the Septuagint (the Greek translation of the Old Testament) to denote the sky or the foundations of the world, which explains its lasting connection to the idea of cosmic solidity.
G4733.portee: This word invites the Christian reader to examine the quality of their own faith: is it unshakeable and deeply rooted in Christ, or is it wavering and superficial? Paul praises the Colossians for this "firmness," suggesting that it is a mark of spiritual maturity and a fruit of grace. For the disciple, the "firmness" of faith is not a rigid stiffness, but a solid adherence to the truth of Christ, capable of withstanding shocks and the seductions of falsehood.

sens: Man who was baptized by Paul in Corinth
Head of a family whose household was the first converted in Achaia
Man who dedicated himself to serving the believers
G4734.detail: 1. Stephanas is a real person from the apostolic era, a Christian from the city of Corinth whom Paul himself baptized, as mentioned in 1 Corinthians 1:16 where the apostle speaks of his experience of baptizing converts. 2. His family was the first to embrace the faith in Achaia (the Greek region of which Corinth was the capital) and immediately dedicated themselves to serving other believers, as noted in 1 Corinthians 16:15, making it a model household of devotion. 3. At the end of his letter to the Corinthians, Paul mentions the visit of Stephanas, Fortunatus, and Achaicus who brought courage and comfort to the apostle by coming to see him (1 Corinthians 16:17), showing his importance in the early Church.
G4734.origine: The name Stephanas comes from the Greek "stephanos" which means crown or reward, evoking the idea of victory or distinction. This name was common in the Greek world of the time and reflects the hope that the child would be honored or receive blessings. The same Greek word is used to denote the crown of glory or the eternal reward in the New Testament.
G4734.emploi: Stephanas appears four times in the first letter to the Corinthians, always in connection with Paul. Paul first mentions him as one of the few people he personally baptized (1 Co 1:16), then highlights him as the head of the first Christian family in Achaia, fully devoted to serving the saints (1 Co 16:15). He is then cited among those who visited Paul, having supplemented the absence of the Church (1 Co 16:17). These mentions reveal a trustworthy man, from the first apostolic generation, likely a deacon or local leader.
G4734.portee: Stephanas embodies the early believer who immediately moves from conversion to dedicated service. His story encourages Christians to see that real faith is expressed through concrete devotion to others and the community. It also shows how brotherly visits and mutual encouragement are essential to the life of the Church, especially for apostles on mission.

sens: An object that encircles the head, an ornate circle worn as a symbol of dignity or victory
A crown of foliage or metal given as a prize
A symbol of royal power or supreme honor
An eternal reward promised to the faithful
An image of triumph or spiritual glory
G4735.detail:
1. Concretely, a crown is a circular object that encircles the head. It can be made of woven foliage (a victory crown at the games) or precious metal (the insignia of a king). The crown of thorns placed on Jesus' head (Matthew 27:29) is a grotesque and cruel form of it.

2. The crown is primarily a prize, a reward given to the victor at the games or to someone who has accomplished a feat: the runner in 1 Corinthians 9:25 runs to receive a corruptible crown.

3. It also signifies royal authority and dignity. The elders in the vision of Revelation 4:4 wear golden crowns, symbolizing their glorious position before the throne of God.

4. Spiritually, it becomes God's promise to believers: a crown of life for those who persevere (James 1:12), an incorruptible crown of glory reserved for the faithful (1 Peter 5:4).

5. It also represents what the believer is to God: the Thessalonians are Paul's crown of glory (1 Thessalonians 2:19), meaning his honor and joy before the Lord.
G4735.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning 'to encircle, to gird.' Therefore, the primary meaning is 'that which surrounds' (a wall, a crowd). But it quickly specialized to designate the crown, the object that encircles the head. In Hebrew, the words עֲטָרָה (atara) and כֶתֶר (kéter) have similar meanings: the crown as a symbol of royalty or victory. The Greek word easily translated these terms from the Old Testament.
