G4735.emploi: The word appears 18 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Epistles and Revelation. It first concretely designates Christ's crown of thorns (Matthew 27:29, Mark 15:17, John 19:2, 5). Then it takes on a metaphorical and spiritual meaning: the crown as a prize or reward (1 Corinthians 9:25), the crown of glory or righteousness that God promises to the faithful (2 Timothy 4:8, James 1:12, 1 Peter 5:4, Revelation 2:10). In Revelation, the heavenly creatures wear golden crowns, symbols of their glory and participation in God's reign (Revelation 4:4, 4:10, 6:2, 9:7, 12:1, 14:14). The word also gains an emotional meaning: that which is dear to Paul is his crown (1 Thessalonians 2:19, Philippians 4:1).
G4735.portee: The crown reminds the Christian that their faith is not in vain: it leads to a reward. God promises not only forgiveness but honor, glory, and an incorruptible crown for those who persevere to the end (1 Peter 5:4). This image enhances hope: the believer is not a permanent slave but a child called to reign with Christ. It also invites seeing other believers not as rivals but as one's joy, one's crown of glory (1 Thessalonians 2:19). Finally, it ennobles present suffering, as those who endure the spiritual battle receive a crown (James 1:12).

sens: The first deacon of the Church, chosen to distribute aid to widows
A man filled with the Holy Spirit and divine power
One who bore witness to Jesus unto death
A martyr whose faith persecutes Saul, who will become Paul
G4736.detail:
1. Stephen is one of the seven men chosen by the Church in Jerusalem to serve in the distribution of material aid to widows, particularly the Greek widows who were often overlooked: it is a role of service and equity (Acts 6:5).
2. He is not just a simple administrator: Stephen performs wonders and great miracles among the people, showing that he acts by the power of the Holy Spirit, not by his own ability (Acts 6:8).
3. He becomes the first Christian martyr: brought before the Sanhedrin for speaking against the Law and the Temple, he is condemned and stoned; at his death, he sees the resurrected Jesus at the right hand of God and prays the Lord to receive his spirit (Acts 7:59).
4. His faithful testimony and death provoke a great persecution, of which Saul is the zealous instigator; by keeping the clothes of the killers and approving of his death, Saul accumulates guilt that will haunt him before his conversion (Acts 22:20).
G4736.origine: The name comes from the Greek *stephanos*, which literally means 'crowned' or 'one who wears a crown' — an image of victory and honor. It prophetically underscores Stephen's fate: although defeated and killed in the eyes of the world, he is in reality victorious, crowned by God, and his testimony will bear fruit well beyond his death, particularly in the conversion of Saul who will become the apostle Paul.
G4736.emploi: Stephen appears six times in the Acts of the Apostles, always named by his role or his death. First elected as a deacon due to his great faith and personal connection with the Holy Spirit (Acts 6:5), he performs miracles that attest to his spiritual authority and provoke opposition from the synagogues (Acts 6:8-9). Arrested, he gives a long speech before the Sanhedrin recalling the history of Israel, then is condemned and stoned (Acts 7:59). After his death, devout men bury him, showing the respect his martyrdom inspires (Acts 8:2). The persecution caused by his death scatters the believers as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch (Acts 11:19), and Saul, who keeps the clothes of the killers during this stoning, will later testify to his complicity in this murder and his guilt (Acts 22:20).
G4736.portee: Stephen embodies the Christian whose faith produces signs and the word of judgment, but who also accepts suffering and death rather than renounce Jesus. His example shows that the true power of the disciple is not that of the world but that of the Holy Spirit, and that death itself does not have the final word: Stephen sees heaven opened and Jesus at the right hand of God, a sign that his faith is justified. His martyrdom also becomes a seed: it disturbs consciences — particularly that of Saul — and his death unleashes a wave of evangelization that carries the Gospel far beyond Jerusalem. For every believer, Stephen illustrates the call to serve faithfully, to speak courageously, and to not fear death when it comes to witnessing for Jesus.

sens: To place a crown on someone's head, as a sign of victory or honor
To clothe someone with glory and honor in a figurative sense
G4737.detail:
1. In the literal sense, to crown means to place a crown on the head of a victor or an honored person. In 2 Timothy 2:5, the athlete who wins the victory by competing according to the rules receives his crown: it is the concrete reward for his effort and victory.

2. In the figurative sense, to crown means to clothe with glory and honor, as seen in Hebrews 2:7 and 2:9 where Christ is crowned with glory and honor. This is not a material crown, but the exaltation and dignity with which God adorns Him, particularly after His death and resurrection. The image remains that of a crown, a symbol of royalty and victory, but it applies here to the glorious and eternal position of Christ with God.
G4737.origine: The word comes from στέφανος (stéphanos), which means crown. It is a verb formed directly from this noun: to crown is to give a crown or to adorn someone with it. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew verb עָטַר (atar), which also means to crown. The crown itself evokes victory, royalty, honor, and dignity.
G4737.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament. In 2 Timothy 2:5, it refers to literally crowning a victorious athlete. In Hebrews 2:7 and 2:9, the meaning becomes theological: it is Christ who is crowned, not with material crowns, but with glory and honor. In these two passages, the verb expresses the divine exaltation of Christ: God crowned Him after His temporal humiliation and death. The context thus shifts from the athletic domain to the domain of redemption and the heavenly glory of the Savior.
G4737.portee: This verb reminds us that God crowns those who persevere and obey. For the believer, it first evokes the promised reward for those who fight the good fight according to faith. But above all, it reveals that Christ had to go through humiliation and death before being exalted by God and crowned with glory. This teaches that God's victory and honor do not come from earthly power, but from obedience and sacrifice, and that God Himself elevates and honors those who remain faithful to Him.

sens: The front part of the body between the neck and the abdomen
The seat of emotions and moral conscience
A gesture of repentance: to strike one's chest
G4738.detail:
1. The chest is the part of the human body that extends from the neck to the ribs — the ribcage and breasts. It is the physical center of the person. John 13:25 describes the beloved disciple leaning on Jesus' chest during the meal, an image of deep intimacy and trust.

2. In biblical thought, the chest is the place where the heart resides, the seat of conscience, thoughts, and feelings. This is why it often designates the inner and moral person. It represents who we truly are, beyond appearances.

3. Striking one's chest is a traditional gesture of penitence, moral pain, and sincere repentance. In Luke 18:13, the tax collector strikes his chest while confessing his sin before God. This same attitude is found in Luke 23:48, where the crowd strikes their chests after witnessing Jesus' death, a sign of heartfelt conviction.
G4738.origine: The Greek word *stêthos* (στῆθος) comes from an ancient root designating the chest as the center of the visible body. It has no direct equivalent in biblical Hebrew, but it often translates the Hebrew word *lēb* (לֵב), which means 'heart' in the sense of the seat of intelligence and will — hence the link between the chest and moral conscience. The Greek word is very common in descriptions of the body and gestures.
G4738.emploi: The word appears 5 times in the New Testament, notably in the Gospels and Revelation. In John 13:25 and 21:20, it describes the physical intimacy of the beloved disciple with Jesus: leaning on His chest means being very close to Him and trusting Him. In Luke 18:13 and 23:48, *chest* is the seat of the gesture of repentance (striking oneself) — it is an act that expresses moral pain and remorse. In Revelation 15:6, it simply designates the part of the body where angels wear golden sashes, a sign of their dignity. The word thus remains concrete and physical, but often carries moral or emotional significance.
G4738.portee: For the believer, the chest reminds us that the entire body is involved in faith and repentance — it is not a purely mental affair. The gesture of striking one's chest while confessing sin (like the tax collector in Luke 18:13) shows that true conversion traverses both body and soul. The image of the disciple leaning on Jesus' chest also speaks of a tangible and concrete communion with the Lord, not just spiritual. It is a word that roots faith in the real, in the body and its gestures.

sens: To stand upright, to be in an upright position
To remain stable, immobile, without falling
To persist, to maintain a resolution or conviction
To resist pressure, temptations, trials
G4739.detail:
1. The primary and concrete meaning is to stand upright, in a vertical position: in Mark 3:31, Jesus' mother and brothers remain outside, standing to call Him. This is a simple physical description.

2. More broadly, it means to stay in place, stable and immobile, without wavering: in Romans 14:4, Paul speaks of a servant who 'stands' before his master, meaning he remains firm, balanced.

3. The meaning becomes figurative when it designates perseverance in faith or in a decision: in Galatians 5:1, 'stand firm' means not to let go in the face of seducers who would want to bring you back under the yoke of legalism. One must remain firmly attached to the freedom received through Christ.

4. It is also to resist, to hold firm despite spiritual storms: in 1 Corinthians 16:13, the exhortation 'stand firm in the faith' urges not to be shaken by doubts, false teachings, or difficulties.
G4739.origine: The verb στήκω is a later form of Greek, forged from the perfect ἕστηκα ('I stand'), which itself comes from the verb ἵστημι ('to place, to set'). The root evokes the idea of stability and balance: something or someone that 'stands' remains in a fixed, unshakeable position. This verb connects the physical sense (the upright posture) to figurative senses (moral and spiritual firmness).
G4739.emploi: The verb στήκω appears nine times in the epistles of the New Testament and carries two main nuances. First, it literally describes the physical position: to stand (Mark 3:31, Mark 11:25). Secondly, and especially in Paul's epistles, it takes on a figurative and spiritual meaning: to stand firm, unshakeable in faith and Christian convictions (Galatians 5:1, 1 Corinthians 16:13, Philippians 1:27, Philippians 4:1, 2 Thessalonians 2:15). Paul uses it to exhort young churches not to be seduced or troubled: to hold firm in the freedom of Christ, to remain anchored in faith, to resist false teachings. It is a call to moral stability in the face of external and internal assaults.
G4739.portee: For the Christian, this word expresses the fundamental requirement of faith: not a passive adherence or a fragile conviction, but an active and courageous firmness. To stand firm is to refuse to be tossed about by trends, social pressures, or doubts. It is also to remember that our solidity is not primarily in ourselves, but in God: 'If someone falls, the Lord has the power to strengthen him' (Romans 14:4). The Christian faith is not a feeling, but a rooting.

sens: Solidity, stability; the quality of that which holds firmly
Moral assurance, constancy in faith and conduct
G4740.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes the quality of something that is solidly established, that does not waver — the image of a construction or a person well anchored to the ground. It is physical firmness: something that holds strong, that resists.
2. In a moral and spiritual sense, it is inner firmness: the constancy, the stability of one who does not deviate from their path. In 2 Peter 3:17, Peter warns believers not to be led astray by the error of the wicked and not to fall from their "firmness" — that is, from that unwavering conviction and loyalty to the Gospel they have received.
G4740.origine: The word comes from the verb στηρίζω (to affirm, assure, firmly establish), which has its root in the idea of making something stable. The family of the word evokes this notion everywhere: what is "stérigmé" is unchanging, assured. It is a lasting quality, a solid foundation, whether physical or moral.
G4740.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Peter 3:17, in a context of pastoral warning. Peter exhorts the young churches to remain firm in their faith in the face of false teachers and seducers. The "firmness" he speaks of is that which is acquired by remaining in the truth received and refusing to be shaken.
G4740.portee: This term reminds the believer that faith is not a fleeting or fragile adherence, but a solid commitment, a stable position that must be cultivated and defended. Understanding this word helps to grasp that the issue is not having faith at the outset, but keeping it firm in the face of temptations and seductions.

sens: To make solid, stable, immovable
To give firmness to a resolution, to an intention
To confirm, consolidate the faith, hope, or virtue of someone
To establish someone in the truth or in a conviction
G4741.detail:
1. To make solid and stable: the word first depicts the physical action of fixing something firmly in place, like driving a stake into the ground so that it does not move. It is the image of the Lord strengthening "a chasm" between the rich man and Lazarus, in Luke 16:26, so that nothing can cross it.

2. To give firmness to a resolution: to apply this solidity to human will. When Jesus "set his face" to go to Jerusalem (Luke 9:51), he fixed his gaze ahead, immovable in his determination, even knowing what awaited him.

3. To consolidate faith and hope: this is the most frequent sense in the epistles. Paul sends Timothy to "strengthen" the Thessalonians "concerning your faith" (1 Thessalonians 3:2) — not to give them a new one, but to fortify it, like one props up a house that threatens to collapse.

4. To establish in the truth: to confirm someone in what they believe or know. Peter says he will take care to remind his readers of Christian truths, although they are "established in the present truth" (2 Peter 1:12) — it is to keep them standing, unshakeable, in the knowledge of the Gospel.
G4741.origine: The Greek verb στηρίζω comes from a root that evokes the idea of making firm and stable. In the Hebrew of the Old Testament, it often translates verbs like סָמַךְ (to support, to lean) or שׂוּם (to establish, to place). The family of the word includes the noun στῦλος (column, post) and the noun στήριγμα (support, prop). The image is always that of something that holds strong, that does not collapse.
G4741.emploi: The word appears 12 times in the New Testament, mostly in the apostolic epistles and Revelation. It is rare in the Gospels (3 occurrences) where it first describes physical action (fixing a chasm, pressing forward) or a disposition (Jesus' resolution). In the epistles, particularly those of Paul and Peter, its use becomes almost technical for speaking of pastoral work: strengthening believers in faith (1 Thessalonians 3:2, 3:13), comforting and confirming them in good work and word (2 Thessalonians 2:17), or keeping them in spiritual vigilance (Revelation 3:2). The word always expresses an action of support or stabilization, never of creation ex nihilo.
G4741.portee: This word speaks to the Christian about the essential role of mutual support in faith. The Bible shows that faith is not a solitary affair: it needs to be strengthened, recalled, consolidated by the Word, by prayer, by brotherly exhortation. It is a call to perseverance — we must not only believe once, but remain unshakeable. And it is an invitation to serve other believers by strengthening them in their walk, as Jesus said to Peter: "strengthen your brothers" (Luke 22:32).

sens: A visible trace made on the skin, often permanent, like a scar or a burn
A sign engraved in the flesh to identify the owner of a person or property
Figuratively: a visible and lasting proof of what one has endured or what one represents
G4742.detail: 1. A mark is primarily a physical trace, engraved or imprinted on the body in a lasting way. The Greek word particularly denotes marks from piercings (tattoos, scars, brands) that cannot be erased. It is a visible and permanent sign, like a wound that remains. 2. In antiquity, slaves or animals were marked in a way similar to a seal of ownership: this mark indicated to whom they belonged, or served an identification purpose. It was imposed and indelible. 3. Paul says in Galatians 6:17 that he bears on his body "the marks of Jesus": these are the scars, wounds, and injuries he received while proclaiming the Gospel and suffering for Christ. These marks have become for him a kind of seal of his belonging to the Lord and of his total commitment. This figurative sense transforms a physical wound into a badge of fidelity and devotion.
G4742.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to pierce" or "to engrave." The starting image is therefore that of a needle or instrument that pierces and leaves a persistent trace in the skin. In Hebrew, in Song of Solomon 1:11, there is a similar image of small ornaments or small bumps (rendered in Greek by this word): the common idea is that of a visible and lasting mark imprinted on a surface.
G4742.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Galatians 6:17. Paul uses it in the context of his apostolic sufferings: he reminds the Galatians that he has already endured persecutions and beatings for the Gospel, and that his body bears the scars as irrefutable evidence of his devotion to Christ. This choice of the word "marks" (rather than simply "wounds") emphasizes the indelible and public nature of these scars: they are permanent signs, visible to all, that attest to his faithfulness.
G4742.portee: This word invites us to reflect on what it truly costs to follow Jesus and serve the Gospel. Paul's marks are not decorations: they are wounds, sufferings endured out of love for Christ. For the reader, this passage reminds us that authentic faith can involve suffering, and that these wounds can become powerful testimonies of our commitment to God.

sens: A point or a prick
A very short moment, a tiny lapse of time
G4743.detail: 1. The word originates from a physical sense: a prick, a point. This is the basic image — something so small and fine that it is barely pricked. 2. From this arises the figurative sense used in the Bible: an instant, an extremely short moment. In Luke 4:5, the devil takes Jesus to a mountain and shows him all the kingdoms of the earth "in an instant" — the time is so compressed that the vision occurs in a single moment, without appreciable duration.
G4743.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb στίζω (stizô), which means "to prick" or "to pierce." Literally, a stigmé is thus a prick, a mark of a prick. The meaning has refined to designate a geometric point, then an instant — something infinitely small in time, just as a prick is in space. The root evokes the idea of extreme smallness.
G4743.emploi: This word appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 4:5, during the temptation of Jesus in the wilderness. The devil transports him to a high mountain and shows him "in an instant" all the kingdoms of the world. The context emphasizes the supernatural rapidity of this vision: in a single moment, what would be impossible naturally unfolds before Jesus's eyes. The word seeks to express the total absence of duration, the precision of a fleeting instant.
G4743.portee: This word reminds us that God masters time as He masters space. What takes us years can happen in an instant by the power of God. It invites us not to fear temptations or challenges: in the present moment, however brief it may be, we can rely on the presence and strength of God.

sens: To shine with a bright luster
To emanate a brilliant and pure light
To radiate glory or majesty
G4744.detail:
1. The verb στίλβω describes the quality of something that shines intensely, like something polished or luminous that reflects light. In Mark 9:3, it is the extraordinary brightness of Jesus's transfigured garments, so dazzlingly white that no fuller on earth could produce it — it is much more than mere clean whiteness: it is a superhuman radiance.
2. The word evokes a light that emanates, that shines from within or from the surface, a radiant clarity. On the Mount Tabor, Jesus's garments do not reflect an external light: they themselves become a source of transfigured light.
3. By extension, to resplend can express a glory or majesty that is visibly manifested, a brilliance that reveals a superhuman or divine reality — which is the case in this unique appearance of transfiguration in the Gospel.
G4744.origine: The verb στίλβω comes from a Greek root describing the action of shining or gleaming. It belongs to a family of Greek words related to light and visible brightness. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament (the Septuagint), it sometimes renders Hebrew roots like לַהַב (lahab), which also describe a flame or luminous brightness — the common image is that of a perceptible, vibrant, and bright light.
G4744.emploi: The verb στίλβω appears only once in the New Testament: Mark 9:3, during the Transfiguration of Jesus on the mountain. It is a pivotal moment where Peter, James, and John see Jesus glorified, his garments becoming resplendent — a visible manifestation of his divinity and glory. The rarity of the word underscores its importance: Luke and Matthew, who also report the Transfiguration, use different terms, but Mark's choice of "resplend" emphasizes the spectacular and unmatched brilliance of this revelation.
G4744.portee: The Transfiguration shows us that Jesus, in his true nature, is a glorious being whose splendor surpasses what the earthly world can express or imitate. This moment strengthens the disciples' faith by revealing the hidden divinity of the Lord. For us today, it reminds us that Jesus is much more than his ordinary human appearance: he is the Son of God clothed in glory, and one day the redeemed will also shine with his light.

sens: Covered gallery or passage supported by columns or pillars
Sheltered space of a building where people gather
Architectural structure characteristic of the Temple in Jerusalem
G4745.detail:
1. The portico is primarily a specific architectural structure: a covered gallery or passage supported by columns or pillars, allowing movement in shelter. It is the image of the typical Greek building.
2. In practice, it is a social space where people gather to meet, talk, and stay together. In Acts 5:12, the apostles stand together in Solomon's portico, showing that it is a natural and accessible gathering place.
3. In Jerusalem, the word mainly refers to the structures of the Temple: the pool of Bethesda had five (John 5:2), and Solomon's portico was a colonnade running along the Temple (John 10:23). These porticoes are important architectural elements of the sacred topography.
G4745.origine: The Greek word στοά (stoa) is a common term in classical Greek architecture. In Hebrew, it sometimes renders רִצְפָה (ritspa), which designates a pavement or a covered floor. The word comes from a root expressing the idea of extending, covering: the portico is literally a surface or structure that extends and protects.
G4745.emploi: The word appears only four times in the New Testament, always to describe concrete places in Jerusalem. At the pool of Bethesda (John 5:2), it refers to the five galleries that surrounded and covered the pool, where the sick waited. In the Temple (John 10:23, Acts 3:11, Acts 5:12), Solomon's portico is the place where Jesus and the apostles walk, teach, or gather. It is always a public, accessible place where the people can approach and where religious activity is manifested.
G4745.portee: The portico reminds us that the encounter with God and the teaching of the Gospel are not limited to the inner sanctuary of the Temple, but unfold in accessible spaces. It is a detail that shows how Jesus and the apostles made themselves visible and available to the people. It also emphasizes the importance of the historical and architectural context: faith is embodied in concrete and tangible places.

sens: Sprig or branch of a plant, particularly of palm or foliage
Flexible plant material that can be cut and transported
Object of celebration and festive joy
G4746.detail:
1. The word designates a branch adorned with leaves, especially from a palm or shrub: it is foliage that can be cut and carried away. In Mark 11:8, the crowds "cut branches from the fields" to spread them on the path before Jesus.
2. What is remarkable is that it is a branch that can be easily cut, not a large tree branch: something that can be pulled and carried by hand, flexible and light.
3. These branches become a sign of joy and honor: spread on the ground, they form a leafy carpet that welcomes the Messiah as a king. It is a gesture of respect and celebration, close to the Feast of Tabernacles where branches of palm and myrtle were carried.
G4746.origine: The Greek word comes from a root that evokes the idea of "to lay down, to spread" (the bed of leaves that is spread out). In Aramaic and Hebrew, the related term designates twigs and braided or arranged branches. It is a concrete word, linked to rural life and the festivals of the Jewish people where vegetation played a central role.
G4746.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Mark 11:8. It is during Jesus's entry into Jerusalem, on Palm Sunday: the crowds cut branches from the fields (probably palm branches and other shrubs lining the roads) and spread them on the path. This act evokes the biblical Feast of Tabernacles and shows how the Jews welcomed Jesus with the traditional signs of honor and messianic joy. The term emphasizes the spontaneous and popular nature of this manifestation: it is not a prepared decoration, but living foliage picked on the spot.
G4746.portee: This branch tells us how a people expressed their joy and respect for the Messiah: not through costumes or learned speeches, but through simple and natural gestures, with the riches of the world that God has created. It reminds us that faith is also expressed in our concrete actions and that the biblical festivals, rich in spiritual meaning, speak to the hearts of believers in a lively and communal way.

sens: The first lesson, the starting point of learning
The elementary principles of knowledge
The material constituents of the physical world
The spiritual powers or laws that govern the world
G4747.detail:
1. The rudiment is the first step in learning, just as the letters of the alphabet are the beginning of reading. In Hebrews 5:12, Paul reproaches Christians for being stuck at the "first rudiments of the oracles of God," when they should be progressing toward a deeper understanding.
2. The word also refers to the elementary principles or basic rules of a discipline or practice. Galatians 4:9 speaks of "weak and beggarly rudiments": Paul criticizes the Galatians for returning to superficial observances instead of living by faith in Christ.
3. In 2 Peter 3:10, "the elements will melt with fervent heat": the word then evokes the physical components of the universe — the substances or forces that make up the world — which will be consumed on the day of judgment.
4. In Galatians 4:3 and Colossians 2:8, 20, the "rudiments of the world" seem to refer to spiritual powers or principles that dominated people before the coming of Christ — religious forces, rules of life, or spirits attributed with governing the cosmos.
G4747.origine: The word comes from the Greek "stoîchos" which means "row" or "line." A stoicheîon is primarily an element of an ordered series: a letter in the alphabet, a step in a progression. The image is that of the first step, the starting point from which the entire structure rises. The family of this word always evokes the idea of a sequence, a progression, an order. In Hebrew, equivalents such as "beginning" or "alphabet" are found, sharing this notion of foundation and starting point.
G4747.emploi: The word stoicheîon appears seven times in the New Testament. In Hebrews 5:12, it refers to the first principles of divine revelation — spiritual milk compared to solid food. In Galatians 4:3 and 4:9, Paul uses it to describe the legal or religious observances of paganism and ceremonial Judaism, from which the Galatians were escaping by faith in Christ. In Colossians 2:8 and 2:20, the context is similar: Paul warns against false wisdom that relies on these "rudiments of the world." In 2 Peter 3:10 and 3:12, the meaning changes: "elements" refers to the physical constituents of the universe (heavens, matter) that will be destroyed. Paul thus contrasts superficial rudiments with spiritual maturity; Peter speaks of the material dissolution of the cosmos.
G4747.portee: Understanding this word helps the reader grasp Paul's critique of attachment to external rules and the principles of the world without Christ. It shows that the Christian faith is not a beginning to surpass, but rather a progression from the superficial to the profound, from the letter to the spirit. For the believer, it is an invitation not to stop at the fundamental elements of the knowledge of God, but to advance toward spiritual maturity and freedom in Christ.

sens: To stand in line, to advance in an orderly and aligned manner
To follow a direction, a path, a determined way
To observe a rule of life, to conform to a principle or standard
To progress together in a common spiritual or moral direction
G4748.detail:
1. The literal meaning is that of a line of soldiers or people advancing in formation: it is the image of military formation, of strict order. In Acts 21:24, the Apostle Paul conducts himself as an "observer" of the law, meaning he follows the law as one follows a drawn line, with regularity and discipline.
2. To walk according to a rule or a way means to orient one's life according to an established principle. In Romans 4:12, believers "walk in the footsteps" of Abraham's faith: they do not deviate, they remain on the same path as he did.
3. To observe a rule of life is to submit to a moral or spiritual standard: in Galatians 6:16, "to follow this rule" refers to adherence to a principle of conduct, an accepted course of action.
4. To walk together, in step, is to progress in harmony in the same direction: in Philippians 3:16 and Galatians 5:25, it is about not being led astray to the left or right, but advancing according to the Spirit, in unity.
G4748.origine: The word comes from στοῖχος (stoïchos), which means "row" or "line." It evokes the image of a troop marching in formation, each person in their place, neither ahead nor behind. The root refers to order and alignment. In late Greek, the word took on figurative meanings: "to walk by rule," "to conform to a standard." It is a common verb among moral writers, to describe one who follows a principle or discipline of life.
G4748.emploi: The verb appears only 5 times in the New Testament, always in Paul: Acts 21:24, Romans 4:12, Galatians 5:25, Galatians 6:16, Philippians 3:16. In each case, it denotes conformity to a rule or spiritual direction. In Romans 4:12, it is about walking in the footsteps of Abraham and his faith. In Galatians 5:25 and 6:16, Paul exhorts the churches to walk according to the Spirit and to follow a given rule. In Philippians 3:16, he invites believers to advance together, without division. The meaning does not vary: it is always an orderly conduct, aligned with a model or principle.
G4748.portee: This word reminds believers that the Christian life is neither chaotic nor arbitrary: it follows a line, that of the Spirit and the will of God. To walk according to a rule is to accept not to be the sole decision-maker, but to align oneself with what has been established by God. It is also an invitation to unity: to walk in step is to refuse division and to progress together toward the same goal.

sens: long and loose garment, generally worn on solemn occasions
festive or ceremonial attire
distinctive sign of dignity or function
heavenly or glorious garment in apocalyptic visions
G4749.detail:
1. In a concrete sense, the robe is a long and flowing garment, worn especially on important occasions. The scribes like to "walk around in long robes" to appear dignified and attract respect (Mark 12:38); the father of the prodigal son orders that "the best robe" be brought to celebrate the son's return (Luke 15:22).

2. The robe also signifies festive attire, the garment that distinguishes the wearer. In the apocalypses, martyrs and the elect wear "white robes," symbolizing purity and heavenly victory (Revelation 6:11; 7:9).

3. It can mark a function or an honorary status: the young man at the tomb, dressed in a "white robe," thus distinguishes himself as a celestial being (Mark 16:5).

4. In Revelation, the robe becomes the image of the glorified state: the elect before the throne wear "white robes," signifying their acquired holiness and eternal communion (Revelation 7:13-14).
G4749.origine: The Greek word comes from a root meaning "to send" or "to equip," and primarily denotes equipment, armament, then clothing. It translates in the Greek Old Testament the Hebrew בֶּגֶד (beged), the ordinary garment, and also לְבוּשׁ (levosh), clothing in a broad sense. It is a noble and solemn word, emphasizing less the simple fabric than the dignified bearing and social function of the garment.
G4749.emploi: The word appears 9 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Revelation. In Luke and Mark, it refers to the long garment that the scribes wear with vanity in daily life (Mark 12:38; Luke 20:46), or the festive robe worn by a distinguished host (Luke 15:22). In Revelation, it takes on a mystical dimension: martyrs and the multitude of the elect wear white robes symbolizing victory and eternal purity (Revelation 6:11; 7:9, 13-14; 22:14). The context shows that the robe is never a simple garment, but always a sign: of dignity, of heavenly honor, or of earthly vanity.
G4749.portee: For the Christian, the robe invites reflection on what one displays of oneself: the scribes seek long robes for the glory of men, a vanity that Jesus denounces. At the same time, the image of the white robe in Revelation promises the believer a heavenly glory, not earned by oneself, but given by God. It reminds us that our true honor does not come from earthly appearances, but from our justification in Christ and our calling to holiness.

sens: The opening of the face through which one speaks and eats
The jaw, the mouth of an animal
The entrance, the opening of something (river, sword)
The organ of speech, what comes out of the mouth when one speaks
The word, what is said or declared
That by which God speaks, His revealed message
G4750.detail:
1. The mouth is the physical opening of the face. Matthew 15:11 speaks of what enters and exits the mouth to characterize moral impurity. In Matthew 4:4, it is the word of God that comes from the divine mouth.
2. For animals, the mouth becomes the jaw: in 2 Timothy 4:17, Paul mentions his deliverance from the mouth of the lion, meaning the danger of death.
3. By extension, the word designates any gaping opening: in Revelation 12:16, the earth opens its mouth to swallow the river. The sword has an edge, referred to as the mouth of the sword in figurative language (Hebrews 11:34).
4. The mouth is primarily the seat of speech: Matthew 12:34 states that it is out of the abundance of the heart that the mouth speaks. In Luke 6:45, the words of the heart come out of the mouth.
5. By metonymy, the word mouth signifies the word itself, the discourse: Romans 10:8-10 plays on this equivalence between confessing with the mouth and believing with the heart.
6. Finally, mouth designates the means by which God speaks: Luke 1:70 and Acts 3:21 refer to what God has said "by the mouth of His holy prophets." God conveys His revelation through the mouths of His messengers.
G4750.origine: The Greek word stoma comes from a root that designates the opening, the mouth in the most physical sense. In ancient Hebrew, we find peh, which literally means "mouth" but also extends to the idea of opening, entrance, or end. The Greek translation of the Old Testament uses stoma to render peh in almost all cases. The word has retained its primary concrete meaning while enriching itself with figurative meanings, notably that of word or message, linked to the fundamental role of the mouth in communication.
G4750.emploi: Stoma appears 72 times in the New Testament, mainly in Luke and Revelation. Its usage oscillates between the literal sense and the figurative sense. In Matthew, Jesus uses it to speak of impurity (15:11, 15:18) and the heart (12:34). In Luke and Acts, it often designates the mouth as the organ of preaching and prophecy: Luke 1:70, Acts 1:16, 3:21. Paul uses it theologically in Romans 10:8-10 (the confession with the mouth and the faith of the heart). Revelation, very visual, multiplies the images: a sword coming out of the mouth of Christ (2:16, 19:15), fire and sulfur coming out of the mouths of horses (9:17-18). The word always retains this link between the physical organ and what it expresses or produces.
G4750.portee: The mouth reminds the believer that their words carry weight: Matthew 12:34 teaches that it is from the heart that they proceed. It invites us to examine what comes out of our mouths (Ephesians 4:29, James 3:10), for the word reveals the state of the heart. Moreover, the mouth of the prophets and apostles becomes the channel through which God speaks to His people: Romans 10:9 even makes it the means of the confession of faith that saves. It is also through the proclaimed word that the Gospel bears fruit.

sens: The organ of the body that digests food
The opening or entrance of this organ
In a figurative sense: the capacity to endure or digest something
G4751.detail:
1. The stomach is the internal organ that receives and digests food after it has been swallowed. This is the concrete and medical sense of the word. In 1 Timothy 5:23, Paul advises Timothy to drink a little wine "because of his stomach," meaning to relieve his digestive problems and frequent infirmities.
2. The word originally comes from a root meaning "mouth" or "opening," and it can refer to the opening or cardia of the stomach, its point of entry. This sense was common among ancient Greek medical writers.
3. In a less attested figurative usage, the word can evoke the capacity to endure or digest morally, as one might say "to have the stomach" for something; but this sense remains secondary and underdeveloped in the biblical text.
G4751.origine: The Greek word stomachos derives from the noun stoma (mouth, opening): it literally means "that which relates to the mouth." The root evokes the idea of an opening or passage. In ancient Greek, medical writers, and later writers like Plutarch, used it to refer to the stomach itself, the organ where food enters and digestion begins. It is a technical term borrowed from Greek medical vocabulary.
G4751.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: in 1 Timothy 5:23. In this passage, Paul writes to his young collaborator Timothy, who seems to have digestive or intestinal problems, and advises him not to drink only water but to use a little wine "because of his stomach" and his frequent ailments. It is a kind pastoral advice, blending concern for health and sobriety: Paul acknowledges the realities of the human body and does not prohibit wine for medical purposes, contrary to strict abstinence. The word is technical and medical, rarely used elsewhere in Greek biblical texts.
G4751.portee: This verse reminds us that the Bible does not despise the body or its concrete needs. Paul treats Timothy with care, recognizing that illness and physical weakness are real, and proposing a wise and measured remedy. This teaches us that taking care of our health, eating, drinking with sobriety, and seeking reasonable means to relieve suffering are acts in accordance with God's will. The Christian faith does not exclude prudence or kindness towards our bodies.

sens: Military expedition or campaign
Armed confrontation, battle
Struggle, resistance against a hostile force
Spiritual engagement against evil and error
G4752.detail: 1. In its primary and concrete sense, a strategy refers to a military expedition or a campaign conducted by an army — the entirety of organized war operations to conquer or defend a territory (the original image: this word comes from the root that speaks of the army, the camp). 2. More broadly, it is the armed confrontation itself, the fight that warriors engage in. 3. Figuratively, it is any struggle, any resistance against a hostile force or an obstacle that opposes us. 4. In Paul's letters, the word takes on a spiritual significance: it is the Christian's commitment against evil, error, and opposing spiritual forces. In 2 Corinthians 10:4, Paul asserts that "the weapons we fight with are not carnal" — he speaks of the spiritual battle of the missionary, not ordinary warfare. In 1 Timothy 1:18, Timothy is called to "fight the good fight": it is the struggle for true faith, the guardian of the Word and the Gospel.
G4752.origine: The word comes from the Greek root that speaks of the army, the military camp (strategos, the one who commands the army, and strateuein, to campaign). In Hebrew, it often translates the word tsava, which designates both the army and the expedition, the service of the soldier. Greek uses this same concrete word to express, in a figurative sense, the spiritual battle — the war of the soul against sin and lies.
G4752.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament, both times in Paul, and always in a figurative sense: never to designate an ordinary battle. In 2 Corinthians 10:4, it is the missionary's fight for the Gospel, conducted by the Word and prayer, not by coercion or carnal violence. In 1 Timothy 1:18, it is Timothy's personal commitment to keep the true faith against heresy and doctrinal error. Paul borrows the soldier's image from battle to show that the Christian life is a serious, demanding struggle that requires vigilance and tenacity.
G4752.portee: This word invites the Christian to take their faith seriously: it is not a passive possession, but an active commitment, a daily resistance against evil and error. Paul uses the image of the fight to show that this struggle is not carnal — it is won not by brute force, but by trust in God and obedience to the Word. This calls every believer to be vigilant, courageous, and faithful in their spiritual life.

sens: A group of soldiers organized into combat units
A corps of troops under a single command
A group of warriors or fighters
Military force sent on a mission
G4753.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a complete army, an organized military force. In Matthew 22:7, the king sends his "armies" to destroy the murderers and burn their city: this is the instrument of royal power to wage war. In Revelation 19:14, the armies of heaven following the Messiah on white horses evoke the same idea of an organized and disciplined force serving a leader.
2. The word can also simply refer to a group of soldiers, a troop. In Acts 23:10 and 23:27, the Roman tribune sends down his "soldiers" to control a riot: these are not entire armies, but military detachments. Acts 23:10 clearly shows this: the soldiers arrive to extract Paul from the angry crowd and escort him safely to the fortress.
3. In Luke 23:11, the word takes on a less strict meaning: Herod's "guards" who mock Jesus do not form an army in the technical sense, but a body of royal soldiers. This is where the translation "mockery" appears in the Segond: not that it is incorrect, but it reflects the context where the army treats Jesus with disdain.
4. In Revelation 9:16, the infernal army counts two myriads of myriads of horsemen: this fabulous number evokes a warrior multitude so vast that it defies calculation, an image of the power deployed against the people of God.
G4753.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb "strateuô" (to fight, to campaign) and the root "stratos" (army, camp). It is close to "strateia" (military expedition, campaign) and "strategos" (general, commander). In Hebrew, the equivalent word is often "tsaba" (army, troop, legion), which designates both the earthly army, the heavenly powers, and even the stars as the "host of heaven." This richness of meaning is found in the Greek of the New Testament.
G4753.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Revelation. In Matthew 22:7, it refers to the royal army sent to punish the rebels. In Luke 23:11, it is the king's personal guard surrounding Jesus. In Acts 23:10 and 23:27, it is the contingent of Roman soldiers intervening to maintain military order. In Revelation 9:16 and 19:14, the word takes on a cosmic and eschatological dimension: the heavenly armies accompanying Christ at the end of times. This progression from the concrete (earthly soldiers) to the celestial image shows how the Bible elevates military language to speak of Christ's final victory.
G4753.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that Christ has a heavenly army far more powerful than all earthly forces. When Revelation describes the armies of heaven following the Lamb, it assures the persecuted believer that God has incomparable power to defend His own and fulfill His plan of salvation. It is an antidote to fear in the face of the powers of the world.

sens: To serve as a soldier, to wage war
To fight in the literal sense, to confront the enemy in battle
To carry out a charge, a military function
To struggle, to oppose with force
To fight spiritually, to wage war against sin and the powers of evil
G4754.detail:
1. To serve as a soldier in an army: this is the literal meaning of the word, which primarily designates one who engages under the authority of a military leader. In Luke 3:14, John the Baptist gives instructions to the soldiers who come to him, showing that they are men enlisted under an authority. This is also the meaning in 2 Timothy 2:4, where the soldier must not be distracted by civilian affairs: his duty is to please the one who enlisted him.
2. To fight means to participate in an armed confrontation. The word evokes the effort of one who exposes himself to battle for the cause he defends. In 1 Corinthians 9:7, Paul uses the image of a soldier who does not serve at his own expense: he must be paid, for the fight puts him in danger.
3. To fight spiritually: the Bible regularly uses this word to describe the believer's struggle against sin and spiritual forces. In 2 Corinthians 10:3, Paul asserts that our struggle is not according to the flesh, meaning that our weapons are not carnal but spiritual. In 1 Timothy 1:18, the fight Timothy must wage is a fight of faith. In James 4:1, the passions that wage war in our members are like an inner conflict.
4. To struggle, to oppose with force: this is the general idea of resistance and conflict. In 1 Peter 2:11, the desires of the flesh wage war against the soul of the believer — they are in opposition, they attack each other.
G4754.origine: The word comes from στρατός (army, troop raised), which evokes the image of a group of armed men ready for battle. The root refers to military organization, to the order and structure of an organized force. The verb literally means "to be in army," "to act as an army." This is why the Septuagint (the Greek version of the Old Testament) uses it to translate Hebrew words that speak of war, battle, and military service.
G4754.emploi: The word appears 7 times in the New Testament. In the Gospels and the letters of Paul, it primarily designates the concrete service of the soldier (Luke 3:14 and 2 Timothy 2:4), with the idea that the soldier is entirely dependent on his leader and must devote all his attention to him. Paul also uses the image of military combat to explain the work of the apostle and the Christian minister (1 Corinthians 9:7), showing that one who works in the service of the Lord has the right to support. Starting from 2 Corinthians 10:3, the word shifts to a spiritual meaning: Paul speaks of fighting not according to the flesh, meaning with spiritual and not temporal weapons. This image becomes central in the pastoral epistles (1 Timothy 1:18) and in the letters of Peter and James, where it describes the believer's inner struggle against sin and passions. The word thus gradually shifts from military concrete to spiritual figurative.
G4754.portee: This word reminds the believer that his life is not neutral: there is a battle being fought between good and evil, between the Spirit and the flesh. It is an invitation to take this internal struggle seriously and not to be distracted by the concerns of the world. The image of the soldier also teaches that the Christian is enlisted under the authority of Christ and must devote his energy to Him without reserve, just as a soldier cannot share his allegiance. This gives meaning to spiritual combat: it is not a defeat or guilt, but a normal reality of the life of faith.

sens: Military chief commanding an army or troops
Civil magistrate governing a city or region
Chief responsible for the guard of the Temple in Jerusalem
G4755.detail:
1. The commander can be a military chief: this is the original meaning of the Greek word, which designates one who leads an army into battle.

2. In cities, the word designates a civil magistrate, an officer who governs and maintains public order. In Philippi, the praetors are magistrates of this type: Acts 16:20 shows civil officers judging the affairs of the city.

3. At the Temple in Jerusalem, the commander was the chief of the temple guard. Acts 4:1 and Acts 5:24 show him intervening with the priests to arrest the apostles who were teaching: he was a military leader of the forces guarding the Temple.
G4755.origine: The word comes from two Greek roots: "stratos" (army) and "agein" (to lead, to conduct). The commander is literally one who leads the army. In Hebrew, this word often translates "sar" (chief, prince) or "sagan" (deputy, vicar), which carry the same idea of authority and command.
G4755.emploi: The word appears ten times in the New Testament, almost exclusively in Luke and Acts. It designates the magistrates who judge Paul and Silas in Philippi (Acts 16:20, 22, 35-36, 38): these are Roman praetors who maintain order. It also designates the commander of the Temple (Acts 4:1, 5:24, 5:26; Luke 22:4, 52), who directs the Levitical guards responsible for the security of the sanctuary. Its meaning thus varies between military and civil authority depending on the context.
G4755.portee: This word reminds us that the early Church encountered established authority — civil magistrates and religious authorities — and that the apostles accepted to be judged by commanders, while remaining faithful to their message. It is an invitation to respect constituted authorities, even in conflict.

sens: Organized group of armed soldiers
Large multitude of celestial beings (angels or stars)
G4756.detail:
1. An army is a group of organized and equipped warriors for combat. This is the direct military sense of the word, designating the troops of a kingdom or nation.
2. By extension, the word designates any impressive and organized multitude. The Bible uses it to describe the heavenly army of angels that appears to the shepherds of Bethlehem (Luke 2:13), singing the glory of God. It also applies to the stars in the sky, which some peoples mistakenly worshiped as deities (Acts 7:42: "the army of heaven"). The image remains that of an ordered and impressive multitude.
G4756.origine: The Greek word *stratia* comes from the same root as *stratos* ("army") and *strategos* ("general"). It evokes the idea of a troop arranged in order. In the Greek Old Testament, it generally translates the Hebrew word *tsaba*, which primarily means "army," but takes on a broader sense: "organized multitude" or even "service." The word *tsaba* also designates the heavenly armies — angels and stars — considered to be in the service of God.
G4756.emploi: This Greek word appears twice in the New Testament according to our sources. In Luke 2:13, the heavenly army is the multitude of angels celebrating the birth of Jesus. In Acts 7:42, Stephen refers to the "army of heaven" as the stars that the Israelites worshiped on their way to the promised land — a practice that God had condemned. In this latter case, "army" retains its weight: it is not a mere collection, but an organized, impressive crowd that some peoples have erroneously revered. Both uses emphasize the collective and majestic nature of the term.
G4756.portee: This word reminds us that the entire universe — angels, stars, creatures — is organized in order and in the service of God. It invites the believer to see beyond the visible: the angels form an army of praise, not a chaotic force. It also serves as a warning against idolatry: no creature, even if organized and splendid, should be worshiped — only God deserves this worship.

sens: Armed man in the service of civil or military power, belonging to a regular troop
Fighter in a battle, in a situation of violence
Warrior engaged in a struggle, in a figurative sense
G4757.detail:
1. In the literal sense, a soldier is an armed man who is part of a military organization and obeys his superiors. The centurion in Matthew 8:9 provides the clearest image: he commands soldiers who obey him instantly, illustrating the hierarchical structure and authority that defines military life.
2. The soldier also appears in scenes of violence and conflict: at the crucifixion, the Roman soldiers divide Jesus' garments (John 19:24) and carry out execution orders (John 19:32, 34). They embody brute force in the service of established power.
3. Paul uses the word figuratively in 2 Timothy 2:3: "Share in suffering as a good soldier of Jesus Christ." The believer becomes a soldier, engaged in a spiritual struggle, obeying Christ as a soldier obeys his commander.
G4757.origine: The Greek word στρατιώτης comes from "stratos" (army) and designates one who is part of an organized army. In Hebrew, the Old Testament uses terms like "ish" (man) or "gibor" (warrior) for similar realities, but the Greek context of the New Testament makes the Roman soldier a familiar figure: order, hierarchy, obedience, military discipline.
G4757.emploi: The word appears 24 times in the New Testament, mainly in the Gospels and Acts. In the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John), soldiers are mostly Roman soldiers: they guard Jesus at the praetorium (Matthew 27:27), crucify him, and divide his garments (John 19:2-34). In Luke and Acts, Roman soldiers protect the apostles or transport them (Acts 21:35, 27:32). Only once (2 Timothy 2:3) does Paul transpose the term to the spiritual realm: the disciple must endure suffering as a soldier endures battles. The word always retains the sense of a disciplined man, hierarchically ordered and submissive.
G4757.portee: The soldier in the Bible speaks of the power of this world: its strength, its organization, its authority. By showing soldiers who understand nothing of Jesus and blindly execute orders, the Bible reveals a limit to their power. But when Paul calls the believer to be a soldier of Christ, he invites him to an obedience as radical as that of the soldier — but towards the invisible King and His justice. It is an invitation to spiritual discipline and courage to remain faithful.

sens: to enlist as a soldier, to be recruited into an army
figuratively, to commit to serve someone with dedication
G4758.detail:
1. The word literally evokes the action of enlisting or being raised for military service: a soldier who agrees to join the ranks of an army. It is the image of voluntary or mandatory enlistment.

2. In 2 Timothy 2:4, Paul uses it figuratively to speak of the Christian's commitment to Christ: one who "enlists" with Jesus must not be distracted by the cares of life, but remain faithful to the one who called him, just as a soldier must obey his commander.
G4758.origine: The Greek word comes from two roots: στρατός (the army, the troops) and λέγω (to gather, to collect, to raise). It thus literally means "to gather an army," "to raise soldiers." This military image of commitment is central to its biblical usage.
G4758.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Timothy 2:4. Paul uses this military metaphor to exhort Timothy to be a good servant of Christ. By speaking of one who enlists with a commander, Paul illustrates the idea that the Christian must fully dedicate himself to his service to Jesus Christ, without being diverted by worldly concerns. The context shows that this enlistment requires unwavering loyalty.
G4758.portee: This image of enlistment reminds the Christian that following Jesus is not a superficial or part-time commitment: it is a total engagement, similar to that of a soldier who belongs to his army. It invites clarity of choice and faithfulness, accepting that this commitment involves demands and sacrifices.

sens: military chief who commands a stationed troop
more specifically, the prefect of the praetorium, commander of the Roman imperial guard
G4759.detail:
1. The word designates a military chief who commands a garrison or a fortified camp — literally, one who "commands the camp." This is a high-ranking officer responsible for the order and discipline of a military unit stationed in a city or region.

2. In the Roman context of the New Testament, it specifically refers to the prefect of the praetorium, the supreme commander of the imperial guard of Caesar and his residence in Rome. This is a position of great political and military importance. When Paul arrives in Rome as a prisoner, it is to this commander that he is entrusted (Acts 28:16).
G4759.origine: The Greek word is formed from two elements: "stratopédon" (στρατόπεδον), which means "military camp" or "fortified camp," and "archô" (ἄρχω), which means "to command" or "to lead." Thus, it literally means "one who commands the camp." This composition reveals the Roman military hierarchy and the key role of the commander in organizing stationed forces.
G4759.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 28:16, at the moment when Paul, arrested and brought to Rome to appear before Caesar, is handed over to the guard of the commander of the garrison. This passage shows that even as a prisoner, Paul enjoys a certain consideration: he is not thrown into an ordinary prison, but entrusted to this high-ranking officer. This detail illustrates the respect that the apostle enjoys and also the official position that Rome recognizes for him, since he has appealed to the emperor.
G4759.portee: This word reminds us that human authority, even the most powerful — that of the commander of the imperial guard — is nothing compared to the sovereignty of God. Paul, although a prisoner under the guard of an officer of Caesar, remains free internally and continues to preach the Gospel. It is an invitation to recognize that God controls events far beyond the powers of this world.

sens: Military encampment where soldiers and war material are gathered
Organized group of armed troops
G4760.detail:
1. The word first evokes the image of a military camp: it is the place where soldiers establish themselves, with their tents, provisions, and weapons, organized to fight or lay siege. In Luke 21:20, Jesus speaks of the armies that will surround Jerusalem — he refers to the Roman troops that will besiege the city with all their equipment and discipline.
2. More broadly, the word designates the army itself, the organized group of fighters mobilized and ready to act. It is an organized force, capable of movement and coordinated action, opposing a city or an enemy.
G4760.origine: The Greek word is formed from two elements: "strátos" (the army) and "pédon" (the plain, flat terrain). The starting image is that of an army camped on open ground. It is a common compound in classical military Greek. In the Greek version of the Old Testament, this word often translates the Hebrew "hayil," which designates an army or an organized troop.
G4760.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament (Luke 21:20), but it is in a crucial context: Jesus uses it to announce the siege of Jerusalem by the Roman armies. This is the precursor sign of the destruction of the temple, an event that the disciples fear. The term emphasizes the military and organized aspect of this threat — these are not isolated bandits, but a regular and massive war force.
G4760.portee: This word from Jesus invites the believer to recognize how God fulfills his warnings. It reminds us that the powers of the world, even when organized into formidable armies, remain under the sovereign control of God, who uses them to execute his judgment. It also calls for spiritual vigilance in the face of the signs of the times.

sens: To bend or twist something by wrapping it around itself
To subject to torture by twisting the body
To distort the meaning of a word or writing by misinterpreting it
G4761.detail:
1. In the concrete sense, the word designates the action of bending or twisting an object by wrapping it, as one twists a rope or fabric. The image is that of a force that curves and deforms.

2. By extension, it can refer to physical torture, particularly that which consists of twisting the body to inflict pain: this is the sense found in the texts of conflict between Jews and Greeks reported in the Maccabees.

3. In a figurative sense, the word applies to speech or writing: to twist the meaning means to distort the message by misinterpreting it. This sense appears in 2 Peter 3:16, where Peter reproaches the ignorant for twisting the meaning of Paul's letters, just as they do with the other Scriptures, to justify their own errors and heresies.
G4761.origine: The verb comes from the Greek root στρέφ- (stréph-, to turn, to turn oneself), which evokes the fundamental idea of rotation and bending. The prefix στρεβλ- adds the idea of an abnormal twist, of deformation. The same root is found in other words meaning to turn away, to turn back, or to change direction. The basic image is that of the body or object being twisted until deformed.
G4761.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament: in 2 Peter 3:16. Peter uses it to describe how certain readers, ignorant and unstable, distort Paul's teachings by misinterpreting them, just as they do with the other Scriptures. The context shows that twisting the meaning is a harmful action: it leads to destruction, that is, to wandering and spiritual ruin. It is a deliberate or at least very serious act, which consists of bending the words of the text to extract a meaning that justifies one's own false ideas.
G4761.portee: This word warns us of the danger of interpreting Scripture in a biased way to support our own opinions or errors. Peter shows that reading the Bible while twisting its meaning is not a simple innocent mistake: it is a dangerous deformation that leads to spiritual destruction. The Christian is therefore called to seek the true meaning of the text with humility and sincerity, rather than projecting preconceived ideas onto it.

sens: To pivot the body or head
To direct the gaze or attention towards
To bring back, report back
To change direction or orientation
To convert, change internally
G4762.detail:
1. The most concrete sense: to pivot one's body or head. Jesus "turning" looks at Peter (Luke 22:61), or he "turns" to the crowd (Luke 7:9) — it is the physical movement of the body.
2. By extension: to orient one's gaze or attention. "Present the other [cheek] to him as well" (Matthew 5:39) literally means to turn the other side of the face towards the one who strikes.
3. To bring back, report: when one "returns" something to its starting point, as in Matthew 27:3 where Judas returns the thirty pieces of silver.
4. To change direction or orientation: "Turn around" can mean to abandon one path to take another, in a more general sense of changing course.
5. Figuratively: to convert, change internally. In John 12:40, "to convert" means to transform one's heart and mind, fundamentally changing spiritual orientation.
G4762.origine: The Greek verb στρέφω comes from an Indo-European root expressing the idea of turning or twisting. In ancient Hebrew, the corresponding verb is הָפַךְ (hâphakh), which also means to turn or invert. This image of physical turning naturally extends to internal and spiritual change, hence its use for conversion.
G4762.emploi: The verb appears 22 times in the provided usages, mostly in the Gospels. It is first concrete: the disciples turn to look at Jesus (John 1:38), he turns to speak (Luke 22:61). But it takes on important figurative meanings: turning the other cheek means accepting insult (Matthew 5:39); converting or changing heart is the major spiritual idea (John 12:40). The context often indicates whether it is a movement of the body, gaze, or an internal transformation.
G4762.portee: This verb invites the reader to grasp the link between physical turning and spiritual turning. Turning the body towards someone also means listening to them, paying attention. To convert is an act: to change direction, to turn one's back on sin to face God. For the believer, each "turning" of the body signifies an opportunity to reorient the heart.

sens: To abandon oneself without restraint to wealth, comfort, and carnal pleasures
To enjoy abundance with pride and disregard for judgment
To lead a life of debauchery and sensuality
G4763.detail:
1. To abandon oneself without restraint to wealth, comfort, and carnal pleasures: the verb describes an unrestrained joy in the face of material abundance. In Revelation 18:7, Babylon "has plunged" into luxury, meaning it has fully immersed itself, savoring its limitless prosperity.
2. To enjoy abundance with pride and disregard for judgment: it is not just about enjoying, but enjoying while declaring one's invulnerability. Babylon in Revelation says in her heart: "I sit as a queen, I am no widow" (18:7), mixing luxury and presumption.
3. To lead a life of debauchery and sensuality: the verb encompasses immorality (immoral relationships) and luxury (18:9). It is a lifestyle that rejects all moral and divine restraint.
G4763.origine: The word comes from στρῆνος ("insolence", "delirium"), a root that evokes excess and loss of self-control. The verb appeared in Greek comedies of the 5th-4th century B.C. to describe characters who "abandoned themselves" or "became brazen". In Hebrew, it sometimes translates the sense of enjoying or eating excessively.
G4763.emploi: The verb appears only twice in biblical Greek, both in Revelation chapter 18, where John describes the judgment of Babylon. In 18:7, Babylon itself "has plunged into luxury" with pride. In 18:9, the kings of the earth "have indulged" with her in immorality and luxury. These two occurrences form a coherent picture: luxury is associated with immorality (πορνεία), pride, and blindness to divine judgment. The apocalyptic context gives the word a serious moral weight.
G4763.portee: This word invites the reader to scrutinize their relationship with material pleasures and wealth. It shows how surrendering to greed and comfort can blind a person or an entire society, making them heedless of God's judgment. For the Christian, it is a call to sobriety and vigilance: to enjoy the goods of God, yes, but without forgetting that everything passes and that only God remains.

sens: Excessive wealth and display of well-being
Life of pleasure and debauchery without restraint
Voluptuous refinement that leads to perdition
G4764.detail:
1. The word primarily denotes luxury in the strict sense: the dazzling wealth, the accumulated and displayed material goods. In Revelation 18:3, great Babylon flaunts her luxury, and it is through the power of this luxury that the merchants of the earth have grown rich — it is the ostentatious and showy prosperity of a trading city.
2. But this luxury is not innocent: the word carries the idea of debauchery and moral perdition. It denotes a life given over to pleasure without restraint, to immorality, to the satisfaction of desires. Babylon has indulged in it, and that is what makes her repugnant in the eyes of God.
3. It is an insolent luxury, which displays its rebellion against God. The word suggests arrogance: one enjoys defiantly, lounging in pleasure without fear. It is the luxury of one who believes themselves invulnerable and eternal, ignorant that judgment is coming.
G4764.origine: The Greek word is related to the Latin strenuus (vigorous) but has taken on a pejorative sense: it denotes vigor diverted towards debauchery, energy wasted on pleasures. It is a late word, appearing in the comic poets of Greece around the 4th century B.C. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew שַׁאֲנָן (shaanan), which means "to be at ease, carefree" — the idea of well-being without moral vigilance.
G4764.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Revelation 18:3, at the heart of the vision of the judgment of great Babylon. John depicts the city of the end times, swollen with pride and wealth, which has seduced the whole world with its splendor and pleasures. All — kings, merchants, nations — have been seduced by this debauched luxury. It is precisely this impudent luxury that will be destroyed at judgment. The word concentrates all prophetic criticism: the Babylonian system appears to prosper, but it rests on debauchery and corruption, and it is this insolent prosperity that makes it ripe for destruction.
G4764.portee: This word speaks to the Christian about the traps of material abundance and well-being without God. Babylon symbolizes any seductive system that promises pleasure and wealth while turning away from God. The accumulation of goods, excessive comfort, a life given to desires: all of this seems attractive and powerful, but it is a hidden curse. John warns that this insolent luxury will not last — it will be brought low. For the Christian, it is a call not to be seduced by the attractions of the world, to keep their heart free from attachment to riches and earthly pleasures.

sens: small common bird of little value
G4765.detail: 1. The sparrow is a small ordinary bird, like the sparrow, of no price or importance in the eyes of the world. In Jesus' time, they were sold in lots — two or five sparrows for a penny — so cheap were they (Matthew 10:29; Luke 12:6). Despite this apparent insignificance, Jesus emphasizes that not one of them falls to the ground without God knowing: there is intention, divine vigilance even over what seems worthless.
G4765.origine: The Greek word στρουθίον is the diminutive of στρουθός (bird in general, particularly ostrich). It is a formation that conveys the small and ordinary character of the animal — hence the translation "sparrow". In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew צִפּוֹר (tsippor), which designates small birds in general.
G4765.emploi: The word appears only four times in the New Testament, all occurrences found in the teaching of Jesus in Matthew 10 and Luke 12. Jesus uses it to reassure his disciples about divine providence: if God cares for birds of no commercial value, without price, he will certainly care for his disciples. It is an argument a fortiori — from the lesser to the greater: if the least matters to God, the greater (you, his children) matters infinitely more. The sparrow embodies the humble, the neglected, the fragile.
G4765.portee: This word invites the Christian to understand that God neglects nothing and no one. If his providence extends even to the small birds sold for nothing, it also envelops our worries, our fears, our lives. It is an invitation to abandon fear and to trust — not in the absence of suffering, but in the vigilant presence of the Father who sees and counts every hair on our head (Luke 12:7).

sens: To deploy, unroll something on a surface, especially a fabric or garment
To strew, scatter something on the ground
To prepare, furnish a place by equipping or arranging it
G4766.detail:
1. To spread out means to deploy or unroll a flexible object on a flat surface. It is the physical action of making something occupy more space by opening it or laying it flat. When Jesus entered Jerusalem, the crowd "spread out" their garments on the road (Matthew 21:8), an act that lays them horizontally to cover the ground.
2. To strew means to scatter pieces or elements that spread here and there on the ground. The same event shows the people who "strewed" the road with cut branches (Matthew 21:8): it is not just about placing the branches, but spreading them in a way that covers the path.
3. To prepare and furnish a place means to equip the space by furnishing or arranging it. A "furnished" or "ready" room (Mark 14:15) is a room whose floor is covered with rugs and the seats are adorned with cushions. Similarly, when Peter tells Aeneas to "make his bed" (Acts 9:34), he is asking him to get up and tidy his resting place.
G4766.origine: The Greek verb στρώννυμι comes from a root that fundamentally means "to spread out" or "to lay flat." It translates the Hebrew forms of the verb יַצַע (yatsa'), which carries a similar idea of deployment and arrangement. The word belongs to a family of Greek terms describing the arrangement of objects and spaces, including the preparation of furniture and fabrics. Its usage covers both the concrete gesture (laying down a garment) and the action of arranging (preparing a room).
G4766.emploi: This verb appears five times in the New Testament, exclusively in the Gospels and Acts. Two usages describe the triumphant welcome of Jesus in Jerusalem: the crowd "spreads" their garments and "strews" the road with branches (Matthew 21:8 and Mark 11:8), expressing honor and worship towards a king. Two other usages concern the preparation of the Passover meal room, where the verb in the participle describes a "furnished" and ready room (Mark 14:15 and Luke 22:12). The last usage in Acts 9:34 uses the verb for the arrangement of a sick person's bed. The word thus retains its basic meaning across all these usages: to arrange, to prepare a space or an object.
G4766.portee: This verb, although simple, carries spiritual meanings in the Bible. The action of spreading garments and branches on Jesus' path expresses the honor, worship, and submission of the people towards the one they recognize as king. For the Christian reader, it reminds how a true encounter with Jesus compels one to offer their possessions and respect. The preparation of a furnished room also symbolizes welcome and hospitality, central values in the new life that Jesus inaugurates.

sens: Deserving to be hated, provoking disgust and rejection
Inspiring aversion due to morally repugnant character
G4767.detail:
1. The word describes something or someone who has become worthy of hate due to their behavior or nature. In Titus 3:3, Paul applies it to Christians themselves before their conversion: they were "worthy of being hated" because they lived in wickedness, envy, and desires, which made them truly repugnant in the eyes of God and men.

2. The word does not simply describe a fleeting opinion, but an objective judgment: those who act this way place themselves in a position where hatred towards them is justified and legitimate. This is why Paul uses it to show the seriousness of the sinner's state before grace.
G4767.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb « stugéô » (to hate, to have in abomination) and receives the suffix « -tos » which marks what deserves an action or judgment. It shares the same root as « stugos » (hate, abomination). The word evokes a visceral hatred, a deep rejection provoked by something morally or spiritually disgusting.
G4767.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Titus 3:3. Paul uses it in a context recalling the sinful past of Christians: before knowing Christ and the grace of God, those who become Christians were themselves in a state that made them "worthy of being hated." It is a strong word that emphasizes the contrast between what they were and what they have become by mercy.
G4767.portee: This word reminds Christians of the seriousness and reality of sin: selfish behavior, desire, envy, and wickedness truly place a person in a situation that provokes just aversion. It is also a call to humility: Paul says "we too"—he includes all believers—to show that no one escapes this condition before grace. This word helps to understand the extent of what we have been saved from.

sens: To have a dark, dull, or threatening appearance (of the sky, of the face)
To express through appearance sadness, affliction, or dismay
G4768.detail:
1. The word first describes the physical aspect of something that appears dark, dull, or threatening. When Jesus speaks of the sky in Matthew 16:3, he says that the sky "is dark" — not absolutely black, but of a dull reddish hue that signals a storm. It is the observation of a visible change in appearance.
2. The word also applies to a person's face or expression. In Mark 10:22, the rich young man "saddened" by Jesus' teaching on renouncing wealth sees his face become darkened, overshadowed by sadness: his outward appearance betrays his inner turmoil. It is the face of someone whose soul is darkening.
G4768.origine: The word comes from the Greek adjective « dark, dull » (stugnos), which evokes an obscure or morose hue. The root carries the idea of an appearance that does not shine, that is veiled or tarnished. It is a rare verb, formed to precisely describe how something "becomes dark" or "takes on a dark look" — not total darkness, but a loss of brightness and clarity.
G4768.emploi: The verb appears only twice in the New Testament, in two distinct contexts that show its versatility. In Matthew 16:3, Jesus uses it to describe the appearance of the sky before a storm — the meteorological phenomenon of the sky becoming dull and threatening. In Mark 10:22, the same verb depicts the darkening of the rich young man's face in response to the demand for renunciation — an affliction so vivid that it is visible on his features. The word thus connects the physical (appearance) and the emotional (the sadness that this appearance expresses).
G4768.portee: This word reminds us that our inner emotions are reflected on our faces. It is an invitation to authenticity: we cannot always hide what troubles us. For the rich young man, his darkened face reveals that his attachment to wealth prevents him from following Jesus — the visible sign of a divided heart.
