At the same time, the image of the dark sky invites us to scrutinize the signs that God places before us, rather than remaining blind to the calls of his grace.

sens: Vertical structure that supports a building
Person who plays a role of support or stability in a community
Support or foundation of an immaterial reality
G4769.detail:
1. A column is a vertical structure made of stone or other material, erected to support the weight of a roof or vault. It evokes solidity, permanence, and the ability to bear weight. In Revelation, the mighty angel has "feet like pillars of fire" (Revelation 10:1): the image of a column reinforces the impression of imposing strength and stability.
2. By extension, a person becomes a "column" when they stand firm, immovable, unshakeable in the face of challenges in a community. James, Cephas, and John are called the "pillars" of the Church (Galatians 2:9): they are not weak sticks, but men upon whom one can lean, pillars of faith and unity.
3. A truth, a value, an institution needs columns — solid foundations upon which to rest. The Church is "the pillar and ground of the truth" (1 Timothy 3:15): it is not the roof or the walls, but what supports and upholds the truth of God in the world. In heaven, the believer who overcomes will become "a pillar in the temple" (Revelation 3:12), a symbol of eternal stability and closeness to God.
G4769.origine: The Greek word στῦλος comes from an Indo-European root expressing the idea of "to erect" or "to stand up." It primarily translates the Hebrew עַמּוּד (ammoûd), which has exactly the same meaning: a vertical structure that supports. This word has retained its concrete architectural meaning throughout antiquity before gradually taking on a figurative value to designate any person or institution that stands firm, supports, or preserves.
G4769.emploi: The word "column" appears 4 times in the New Testament, always in these four verses. It is always an image, never a concrete architectural column. Two usages are personal: James, Cephas, and John, three influential apostles, are described as the "pillars" of the Jerusalem Church (Galatians 2:9), meaning its major supports. One usage is institutional: the Church itself is "the pillar and ground of the truth" (1 Timothy 3:15), it upholds and preserves the revelation of God. The two apocalyptic usages describe heavenly visions where the column symbolizes unshakeable power (the feet of the angel) and the eternal stability of the glorified believer in the divine temple.
G4769.portee: This word invites the Christian to reflect on their own role: are we a "column" for others, someone on whom they can lean? It is also a call to recognize that the Church, despite its weaknesses, bears the formidable responsibility of keeping the truth of the Gospel alive and straight. For the one who overcomes, the promise of being "a pillar" in the temple of God evokes a stability and closeness to God that nothing can ever shake.

sens: Belonging to the Stoic school, a Greco-Roman philosophical movement
Professing a wisdom based on virtue and control of passions
G4770.detail:
1. Stoicism is a philosophical school that originated in Greece and was very influential in the Roman world during the time of the New Testament. It taught that virtue is the only true good and that the wise person must live in accordance with the universal reason that governs the cosmos. In Acts 17:18, the Stoics of Athens represent human wisdom in the face of the Gospel: they are respected thinkers who claim to access truth through reason.
2. More broadly, the term designates a philosophical attitude: one who practices Stoicism seeks to dominate their emotions and desires through reason, accepting with serenity what they cannot control. This moral discipline characterizes the Stoic spirit.
G4770.origine: The Greek word Stōikos comes from Stoá, the portico in Athens where the founder Zeno taught his philosophy. It is borrowed from the historical and cultural context of classical Greece. The French term "stoïcien" derives directly from it. Stoic philosophy opposes Epicureanism, the other major materialistic school of the time, and offers an alternative to Christian thought on the question of happiness and the good.
G4770.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 17:18, during Paul's visit to Athens. There, the Stoics are among the philosophers with whom Paul discusses at the Areopagus. Far from the Gospel, Stoic wisdom rests on human reason and the impersonal cosmic order, not on the revelation of God. The text stages the clash between the preaching of the Resurrection (based on God's historical action) and pagan wisdom.
G4770.portee: This unique mention shows Christian readers that human philosophy, even the noblest and most systematic, remains incapable of knowing God and His Resurrection. It invites recognition that faith in Christ is not built on reason alone, but on revelation and the Holy Spirit. The Stoic in Athens, however wise he may have been, needed to hear the Gospel.

sens: Second person singular or plural personal pronoun, designating the one or those being addressed.
Used in the nominative to emphasize or create a contrast with another person.
Placed before an address or invocation to give emphasis to the word.
G4771.detail:
1. As a personal pronoun, this word simply designates the person or people being spoken to. It can be a subject ("you do"), direct object ("I see you"), indirect object ("I speak to you"), or possessive ("your house"). In Matthew 1:20, the angel says to Joseph: "do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife" — the word refers to Joseph himself and what belongs to him.
2. When this pronoun appears in the nominative (the subject form) where it would not normally be expected, it is to create emphasis or contrast: "It is you who do this, not another." John 1:30 is a good example: "This is he of whom I said: After me comes a man who has preceded me." The pronoun "you" appears strongly to highlight the identity of the one being referred to.
3. Before an invocation or direct address (vocative), this pronoun reinforces the personal address: Acts 1:24 shows the apostles in prayer: "Lord, you who know the hearts of all" — the "you" establishes an intimate and respectful relationship with God.
G4771.origine: This word comes from the ancient Indo-European stock that gave rise to personal pronouns in all classical languages. In ancient Greek, it appears in various forms depending on its grammatical role: "σύ" in the nominative (you), "σοῦ" in the possessive genitive (your), "σοί" in the dative (to you), "σέ" in the accusative (you). This paradigm is sometimes enclitic (attached to the preceding word), except after a preposition like "πρὸς σέ" (to you). In Hebrew, the same pronoun is expressed by "אַתָּה" (atta) for singular and "אַתֶּם" (attem) for plural.
G4771.emploi: This word is among the most frequent in the New Testament: it appears more than 2000 times in various forms. It can be found everywhere, in every book and context, as it is the fundamental means of addressing someone. In the Gospels, Jesus uses it when speaking to His disciples, His adversaries, and those He heals. In the epistles, Paul uses it to address his readers directly: "If others enjoy this right over you, should we not rather have it?" (1 Corinthians 9:12). The word can be explicit or implicit (in the verb), and the emphasis placed on the nominative form creates a rhetorical effect — highlighting who is truly responsible or at fault. Mark 8:17 shows Jesus addressing His disciples: "Are you still without understanding?" The "you" makes the address direct and personal.
G4771.portee: For the Christian reader, this simple pronoun reminds us that the Bible is not an abstract word, but a word addressed personally. When Jesus says "you," He addresses each individual. When Paul writes "you," he includes us in his Church. This word creates a relationship — between God and man, between the speaker and the listener. It is a tool of the Gospel: God's grace, Jesus' love, the Lord's commandments are not stated from on high, but addressed to "you" personally, establishing a real encounter.

sens: Blood relationship that unites members of the same family
Group of close relatives
G4772.detail:
1. The word describes the familial bond that connects people of the same blood. Elizabeth and Zechariah ask Mary what name to give her newborn son, and note that "there is no one among your relatives who is called by that name" (Luke 1:61) — they are thinking of all of Mary's cousins, uncles, and other relatives.
2. By extension, it designates all those united by this bond: the family in a broader sense. When God tells Abraham to "leave your country and your family" (Acts 7:3), He asks him to abandon all his close ones. Similarly, Joseph brings "his entire family, consisting of seventy-five people" (Acts 7:14): this includes not just his wife and children, but the entire family clan.
G4772.origine: The word comes from συγγενής ("related"), formed from συν ("with") and γένος ("race, origin"). The basic idea is that of people who share the same origin or blood. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Hebrew word משפחה (mishpaha), which means "clan" or "family" — the fundamental social unit of the people of Israel.
G4772.emploi: The word appears three times in the New Testament, always in the context of very concrete family relationships. In Luke 1:61, it refers to the close circle of Elizabeth's relatives consulted at the time of John the Baptist's birth. In Acts 7:3 and 7:14, it first evokes Abraham's command to leave his family (which marks a radical break with the past), and then the arrival in Egypt of all of Joseph's relatives. In all cases, the word designates a group of people linked by blood, whose size varies according to the context.
G4772.portee: This word reminds us of the importance that the Bible places on family ties and the clan as a unit of life. But the three passages where it appears also highlight that sometimes, to follow God (Abraham leaving his country and kin, or the birth of a son destined to prepare the way for the Messiah), one must accept a break with these ties. Kinship is not an end in itself: it is subject to the call of God.

sens: Member of one's own family, united by blood
Person related by clan or tribe ties
Close one, ally
G4773.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a person united to another by biological kinship: parents, siblings, cousins. Jesus uses it when He says that "a prophet is not without honor except in his own country, among his relatives" (Mark 6:4) — He refers to the immediate family that knew Him as a child.
2. The word can more broadly designate all those who belong to the same extended family or tribal group. Paul uses it when he speaks of his "relatives" according to the flesh in Romans 9:3, encompassing his Jewish compatriots.
3. At its limit, it can simply mean "close one" or "ally" — someone with whom one has a natural and unchosen bond. John 18:26 shows this: the servant who questions Peter is a "relative" of Malchus, the one whose ear Peter had cut off.
G4773.origine: The word comes from the Greek "sun" (with, together) and "genos" (family, race, origin). It literally designates one who shares the same genealogy, the same stock. The Greek of the Old Testament rendered it with Hebrew words like "dod" (uncle or close relative) and "mishpacha" (clan, extended family). The image is that of a common rooting in the same lineage.
G4773.emploi: The word appears 11 times in the New Testament, mostly in the Gospel of Luke (6 occurrences) and in Paul's letters. Luke often uses it to refer to close family: the parents of Jesus who seek Him (Luke 2:44), the relatives of Elizabeth who rejoice (Luke 1:58), or to distinguish relatives from other categories of guests (Luke 14:12). Paul uses it to speak of the Israelites, his compatriots (Romans 9:3), and to designate people related to him by blood or clan (Romans 16:7, 11, 21). The usage remains always concrete: it refers to ties of birth or common descent, never to purely spiritual relationships.
G4773.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible does not despise natural family ties. Jesus Himself spoke of them without reproach, and Paul acknowledged his debts to his people and relatives. But the Gospel also shows that beyond blood ties, other fraternities arise, founded not on genealogy but on faith. This is why we must go beyond mere "sharing of relatives" to build a true community in Christ.

sens: Agreement or permission granted by one who has more authority to one who has less
Concession made out of kindness or indulgence
Understanding compassion towards the weaknesses of others
G4774.detail:
1. Condescension is primarily the agreement that a person of authority or wisdom grants to another. It comes from the heart of one who could demand or prohibit, but who chooses to allow. Paul uses it in 1 Corinthians 7:6 when he says: "I say this by condescension, I do not make it a command" — he explains that his advice on marriage is a tender permission, not a rigid commandment.
2. It is also a concession made out of indulgence: one grants a desire or weakness, not out of obligation, but out of kindness. It is recognizing that the other is not up to a higher ideal, and granting grace for that.
3. More broadly, it is the gentle understanding that the strong manifests towards the limits of the weak — a sympathy that does not condemn.
G4774.origine: The word comes from ancient Greek "sun" (together, with) and "gnômê" (thought, judgment). The image is that of a shared thought or a tender judgment made together. Etymologically, it evokes the idea of a "common thought" that inclines to forgive or to allow. In ancient Greek thought, the word initially meant mutual agreement, then the indulgence and forgiveness granted to one who cannot or does not know how to do better.
G4774.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament: 1 Corinthians 7:6. Paul uses it to qualify his advice on marriage and celibacy. He means that he does not command, but speaks "by condescension" — that is, what he proposes takes into account human weakness and the necessity of marriage for those who cannot remain celibate. It is a rare word, reflecting Paul's pastoral gentleness: he does not want to crush weak consciences under the weight of the Law, but rather to offer them a loving permission that respects their condition.
G4774.portee: This word reveals to the reader God's attitude towards the Church: God is not a judge who crushes, but a Father who "condescends" to our weakness. He grants us permissions, alleviations, because He knows our limits. For the Christian, it is an invitation to imitate this condescension towards others — to be indulgent, to understand, to not burden consciences with a weight they cannot bear. It is also a reminder that grace is not rigidity, but intelligent gentleness.

sens: to be seated with someone
to share someone's seat
to participate in a gathering by sitting together
G4775.detail:
1. To sit with someone means to take a place next to them or in the same location. In Mark 14:54, Peter sits with the servants of the high priest near the fire: he seeks to go unnoticed, blending in among them by sharing their seating position.
2. The word more broadly evokes the idea of sharing space, time, and company with someone. In Acts 26:30, when the king, the governor, and Bernice rise, the text states that they were "sitting with" Paul and the others: it emphasizes that they had gathered together, present together.
3. To sit with can also mean to participate together in a meeting or assembly where one sits side by side, thus sharing a common situation or authority.
G4775.origine: The word combines the preposition "syn" (with) and the verb "káthamai" (to sit, to be seated). This composition creates the idea of closeness and companionship in the act of sitting. The basic image is very simple: two or more people sitting together, face to face or side by side, sharing the same moment and place.
G4775.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In Mark 14:54, it describes Peter sitting with the servants of the high priest's palace to warm himself by the fire while Jesus is being judged: it is a moment of dangerous proximity, where Peter places himself alongside those who oppose the Lord. In Acts 26:30, it refers to all those who were sitting next to King Agrippa during Paul's trial: the emphasis is on the common presence, the assembly gathered to listen.
G4775.portee: This simple verb reminds us that our place, our associations, and our companions reveal our choices. When Peter sits with the servants to warm himself by the fire, he places himself in a posture of abandonment of Christ: the physical detail of sitting becomes the image of faithfulness or unfaithfulness. For the believer, "to sit with" someone means accepting a form of communion or compromise with them.

sens: to sit beside someone
to be seated together nearby
to sit side by side
to share a common position or honor
G4776.detail:
1. The simplest meaning is to sit near someone, as shown by the disciples sitting together around the fire in the high priest's courtyard (Luke 22:55). It is a physical act: to place oneself seated next to another person.
2. This act of being seated together also evokes a proximity of condition or status. When Paul writes that he has made us "sit together in heavenly places" (Ephesians 2:6), he is not simply speaking of physical positions, but of sharing a place of honor, a dignity alongside the risen Christ. It is the image of a common elevation.
G4776.origine: The word combines two Greek elements: "sun" (together, with) and "kathizō" (to sit, to be seated). This combination creates the idea of sitting together, sharing a common seat. The root evokes the act of taking a place, of establishing oneself somewhere. It is a compound word that reinforces the idea of community and participation in a common condition.
G4776.emploi: The word appears twice in the New Testament. First in Luke 22:55, in a very concrete context: the servants and soldiers sit around a fire in the high priest's courtyard after Jesus' arrest. Peter physically joins them, sitting next to them. In Ephesians 2:6, Paul uses the same word in a figurative and spiritual manner: he asserts that God has raised us up together with Christ and made us sit together in heavenly places. The meaning shifts from the physical gesture to the spiritual reality of a co-seating in heaven, a common elevation with the risen Christ.
G4776.portee: This word reminds the believer of two essential things: first, that they are not alone in facing trials or temptations — there is a community of disciples who go through the same difficulties. Secondly, and more profoundly, that if Christ is risen and exalted in heaven, the believer who belongs to Him already shares in His dignity and heavenly honor. It is a promise of participation in the glory of Christ.

sens: to share in another person's troubles
to endure trials together
to take part in the persecutions and difficulties related to the Gospel
G4777.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to share in another person's troubles: to suffer with someone enduring a trial, as one would do together in the same adversity. It is an active compassion, a solidarity in pain.
2. It also refers to enduring difficulties together: accepting one's share of the troubles and mistreatment faced by a group. In 2 Timothy 2:3, Paul invites Timothy to "suffer with me, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ," meaning to accept the same trials as him to remain faithful.
3. In Paul's context, it takes on a specific meaning: to endure with the Gospel the persecutions and rejections it provokes. In 2 Timothy 1:8, Paul asks Timothy not to be ashamed of the testimony of Jesus "but suffer with me for the Gospel," meaning to share in the sufferings caused by the preaching of the good news.
G4777.origine: The word is composed of "syn-" (together, with) and "kakopatheō" (to endure evil, trial). The root "kakos" (evil) evokes a concrete adversity, a difficult trial. The verb thus expresses the idea of shared suffering, of a trial accepted jointly with others.
G4777.emploi: The verb appears twice in the New Testament, both in the letters to Timothy. In 2 Timothy 1:8, Paul exhorts his young collaborator not to be ashamed of the testimony given to the Lord and to him or his message, but to "suffer with" him for the Gospel — it is an invitation to share in the persecutions that Paul suffers for having proclaimed Jesus. In 2 Timothy 2:3, Paul renews his call by inviting Timothy to "suffer with" him as a faithful soldier, placing this shared suffering at the heart of Christian service. The repeated use shows that Paul considers this disposition of heart essential for anyone who assists him in the Gospel.
G4777.portee: This word reminds us that following Jesus is not a promise of comfort, but an invitation to share in the trials He still endures today through His persecuted Church. It invites the believer not to turn away from the one who suffers for the Gospel, but to remain supportive of Him. It is a form of concrete faithfulness: to accept that proclaiming Christ costs and to be willing to pay that price rather than flee from it out of shame or fear.

sens: Share the sufferings and mistreatment of a person or a people
Endure adversity and trials together
G4778.detail:
1. This verb expresses the idea of actively sharing in the sufferings of others. In Hebrews 11:25, Moses chooses to be "mistreated with the people of God" rather than enjoy the pleasures of sin: he voluntarily accepts to live the same difficulties and oppressions as the Israelites, out of solidarity and faith. The image is one of communion in pain, an association in trials.
2. The word emphasizes that this suffering is not passive or endured against one's will, but chosen and shared: it is a form of commitment to those with whom one suffers. The focus is on unity in adversity and the dignity of this trial accepted together.
G4778.origine: The word is composed of the prefix σύν (sun, "with") and κακουχέομαι (kakouchéomai, "to be mistreated, to suffer harm"), which itself is formed from κακός (kakos, "bad, evil") and χέω (chéô, "to hold"). The underlying image is one of "bearing evil together." This term, very rare in biblical Greek, reflects the biblical idea of solidarity in suffering, particularly developed in the New Testament regarding communion with Christ and with the people of God.
G4778.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Hebrews 11:25. It is used to describe Moses' deliberate choice to share in the sufferings of the people of Israel rather than enjoy the temporal pleasures of the Egyptian world. It is in a context of faith and spiritual heroism: Moses renounces immediate advantages to remain faithful to his identity and vocation with God and His people. The word emphasizes the nobility of this decision and its voluntary nature.
G4778.portee: This passage teaches the Christian that true fidelity to God may require renouncing the pleasures and advantages of the world to share in the condition of believers and the values of the Kingdom. Moses becomes a model of one who considers "the reproach of Christ greater wealth than the treasures of Egypt": communion in trial with the people of God is better than solitary prosperity far from Him.

sens: gather people by calling them together
invite friends or neighbors to come share something
officially convene an assembly or council
G4779.detail:
1. Assemble means to call people together in one place. It is a voluntary act: the one who assembles wants to gather people around him. In Mark 15:16, the soldiers assemble the whole cohort — they call them to come together.

2. The word can also refer to the joyful invitation of friends or neighbors to share a happy event. In Luke 15:6 and 15:9, it is the man who has found his sheep and the woman who has found her coin who call their friends to rejoice with them: to assemble is then to invite to the celebration.

3. In an official context, assemble means to solemnly convene an authority, a council, or an assembly. In Acts 5:21, the high priest convenes the Sanhedrin, the assembly of Jewish leaders, for a meeting of power.
G4779.origine: The word comes from "syn" (with, together) + "kaléô" (to call, to summon). It literally means "to call together." The root "kaléô" evokes the act of giving a vocal order to someone to come. In the Greek of the Old Testament, this verb translates the Hebrew "qara" (קָרָא), which also means "to call, to cry out."
G4779.emploi: This verb appears 8 times in the New Testament, mostly in Luke and Acts. In the Gospel of Luke, it describes either the action of Jesus gathering His disciples (Luke 9:1) or the characters in the parables joyfully inviting their friends (Luke 15:6, 9). In Acts, it refers to official convocations: Luke 23:13 shows Pilate assembling the religious leaders and the people, Acts 5:21 the convened Sanhedrin, Acts 10:24 and 28:17 show Cornelius and Paul gathering relatives. The verb can be constructed in two ways: the simple action (assemble a crowd), or the reflexive form (call to oneself, gather around oneself).
G4779.portee: This word shows us how Jesus and His disciples created communion: Jesus assembles His apostles to train them and send them on mission, and in the parables, assembling friends is the very image of shared joy. For us, to assemble expresses the heart of the Christian community — this desire to gather to grow together in faith and celebrate together the works of God.

sens: Cover entirely in a way that conceals
Intentionally hide so that no one sees
G4780.detail:
1. The verb means to cover completely, to envelop with a veil or covering. It is the concrete image: something or someone is covered in such a way as to be hidden from view. The prefix "syn-" (together, completely) reinforces the idea: one covers well, one covers everything.
2. In a figurative sense, the word designates what is secret, intentionally hidden. In Luke 12:2, Jesus states: "Nothing is hidden that will not be made known," meaning that secrets, things one believes can be concealed, will sooner or later be revealed. The emphasis is on the impossibility of lasting secrecy.
G4780.origine: The word is formed from the prefix συν (sun, "together") and the verb καλύπτω (kaluptō, "to cover"). The root καλύπτ- evokes the action of covering, enveloping. In Hebrew, the word כָּסָה (kasah) carries the same meaning: to cover, to conceal, to hide. This verb frequently appears in the Old Testament when speaking of hidden things or what God reveals.
G4780.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 12:2. Jesus uses it in a context of eschatological teaching: He asserts that nothing remains hidden before God, that every secret will be brought to light on the day of judgment. It is a call to sincerity and a warning against hypocrisy: no one can conceal the truth eternally.
G4780.portee: This verse reminds the believer that nothing escapes God's gaze. It invites honesty, before oneself and others, for everything will ultimately be known. This can be both a warning for one who seeks to hide their faults, and a comfort for one who has suffered injustice in silence: the truth will prevail.

sens: bend the body or a part of the body downward
fold or flex completely
submit to a yoke, be weighed down
G4781.detail:
1. Bend primarily means to physically bend: to make the back, loins, or legs flex downward. It is an action of the body that inclines downward due to fatigue, age, or effort.
2. The word also suggests a complete and lasting curvature: not a temporary flexion, but a state where the body remains bent. In Romans 11:10, Paul quotes Scripture saying "let their backs be continually bent" to express persistent dejection.
3. Figuratively, bending evokes the idea of being crushed, submitted, weighed down. A bent back is a sign of a person oppressed, weighed down by misfortune or divine judgment.
G4781.origine: The Greek word συγκάμπτω (sugkamptō) is composed of two elements: σύν (syn, "with, together") and κάμπτω (kamptō, "to bend, to fold"). This composition intensifies the idea of bending: not only to bend, but to bend completely or by folding. In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint), it translates notably the Hebrew verb that also means "to bend" or "to flex" (Psalms 68:10, 23).
G4781.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament: Romans 11:10. Paul cites a passage from the Psalms to describe divine judgment on unbelieving Israel. The expression "let their backs be continually bent" paints the image of a nation weighed down, whose judgment keeps its members in a posture of submission and defeat. The figurative use of the term reinforces the idea of lasting oppression, not momentary.
G4781.portee: This word reminds the Christian of a biblical truth: divine judgment is real and lasting for those who reject the Gospel. At the same time, the citation in Romans 11 is part of a reflection on God's final mercy towards Israel, inviting the reader not to judge harshly those who have fallen, but to await the work of grace.

sens: Go down with someone
Consent to join someone in an endeavor
Agree to lower oneself to someone’s level
G4782.detail:
1. The primary and concrete meaning is to go down at the same time as others: it is a shared physical movement. In Acts 25:5, Governor Festus invites the Jewish authorities to "go down" with him from Caesarea to Jerusalem to accuse Paul before him.

2. The word quickly takes on a figurative meaning: "to condescend," that is, to agree to join someone, to consent to participate in a matter, even if it requires lowering oneself to their level or making an effort. It is an act of goodwill or solidarity.

3. By extension, it also conveys the idea of lowering oneself or consenting to an action one would not ordinarily take, but does so out of regard for others.
G4782.origine: The word is composed of three elements: "sun" (with), "kata" (downward, in descent), and "bainō" (to go, to walk). The basic image is that of a descent accompanied. In ancient Greek, the composition with "sun" (with) indicates an action done in common. The notion of "going down" evokes both a physical movement and, figuratively, a certain humility or self-abasement.
G4782.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament: in Acts 25:5. It is used in its literal and concrete sense. The context shows Festus inviting the Jewish leaders to physically go down with him to accuse Paul. In later Greek authors and biblical Greek wisdom, the word can take on a figurative sense, that of "condescending" or consenting to participate. But in the New Testament, the emphasis remains on the concrete and courteous gesture.
G4782.portee: This word reminds us of the importance of solidarity in movement and common participation in affairs. For the Christian, it also evokes humility: the ability to consent to join others, not out of obligation, but as an act of kindness and sharing. It is a beautiful image of communion and mutual aid in the Church.

sens: agreement, harmony between two things
relationship of concord or understanding
suitable correspondence
G4783.detail:
1. The word denotes the agreement or harmony that exists (or should exist) between two things: a concord, a mutual understanding. In 2 Corinthians 6:16, Paul uses it to express a link or relationship: "What agreement has the temple of God with idols?" — it is about a concordance, a compatibility between two realities.
2. More broadly, the term evokes the question of whether two elements can coexist in harmony: it is the possibility of an agreement, of mutual suitability. Here, Paul poses the rhetorical question to show that there is no possible relationship between what is consecrated to God and what is consecrated to idols.
G4783.origine: The word is composed of three Greek elements: συν ("with"), κατά ("according to, with") and θέσις ("position, placement"). Its basic image is that of a "putting together" or a "joint placement" — the idea that two things are placed in a position of agreement. Related words include σύνθεσις (composition) or θέσις (position). It is a rare word, used in non-biblical Greek writings to describe diplomatic agreements or political concords.
G4783.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in 2 Corinthians 6:16. Paul uses it to explore the theological question of the compatibility between a life dedicated to God and idolatry. It is a term chosen for its strength: it poses the rhetorical question with a word that underscores the absolute impossibility of an agreement, of harmony between these two opposing realities.
G4783.portee: This word reminds the believer that their consecration to God creates a rupture with idolatry and the values of the world that oppose it. Paul's question invites us to examine our own "relationships": are there areas of our lives where we seek a false agreement between authentic faith and spiritual compromises? It is a call to coherence and purity in our commitment to God.

sens: give one's agreement
be in agreement with someone
take part in a decision
associate with an action
G4784.detail:
1. The word literally means "to deposit together" — as if one were placing their vote in a common urn with others. It is the image of active participation, of personal adherence.
2. Figuratively, it expresses the act of agreeing with someone, consenting to their ideas or plans. In Luke 23:51, Joseph of Arimathea "had not participated in the decision and actions of the other" members of the Sanhedrin: he did not approve their judgment against Jesus, he did not associate himself with their vote.
3. More broadly, it is to take part in a collective action or decision — to be involved, to accept to be complicit or responsible.
G4784.origine: The word is formed from three Greek elements: "syn" (with), "kata" (according to, in accordance), and "tithēmi" (to place, to put). The starting image is that of a vote: one places their suffrage together with others. This verb in the middle voice (the reflexive form) means that one deposits their own agreement or responsibility.
G4784.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament (Luke 23:51). It describes Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the Sanhedrin, who distinguishes himself from the others by refusing to participate in the condemnation of Jesus. The usage emphasizes the importance of his courageous position: it is not only about not voting against Jesus, but deliberately standing outside a major collective decision.
G4784.portee: This word reminds the reader that participating in an injustice means being responsible for it. It invites us to examine our own affiliations and complacencies: to what decisions do we give our agreement? Joseph of Arimathea shows that courage sometimes consists of refusing to "participate" with others, even when one is alone.

sens: Count someone among a group by designating them by lot
Assign someone a place in an assembly by a collective choice
G4785.detail:
1. The verb literally means "to vote together with someone": it is the action of counting a person as part of a group, particularly using a collective designation method such as drawing lots. In Acts 1:26, after the apostles' prayer, the lot designates Matthias, who is thus "associated" with the eleven apostles — in other words, integrated by a divine vote, so to speak, into their complete number.

2. More broadly, the word evokes the idea of being admitted or classified in an assembly by a decision that engages the group: it is to receive an official, collectively recognized place within an established community.
G4785.origine: The word is composed of three elements: "syn" (with, together), "kata" (according to, by) and "psēphizo" (to vote, to count votes). The root "psēphos" originally refers to the pebble or ballot that was thrown for voting in Greek assemblies. The verb "psēphizo" thus literally means "to use pebbles or ballots" and, by extension, "to vote." The prefix "syn" adds the idea of doing this together, collectively.
G4785.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 1:26. It describes the moment when the apostles, gathered after Jesus' ascension, seek to fill the vacancy left by Judas' betrayal and death. They pray, then draw lots between two candidates, Joseph Barsabbas and Matthias. The lot designates Matthias, who is then "associated" with the remaining eleven apostles. The context shows that this is a collective and solemn action: the entire assembly, guided by prayer, recognizes Matthias as now part of the group of Twelve.
G4785.portee: This word reminds us that inclusion in the people of God or in His Church is not an individual or private matter, but a collective recognition by the community, often guided by the direction of the Holy Spirit. It also emphasizes that drawing lots, far from being random, is presented in Scripture as a means by which God reveals His will within the believing assembly. Finally, it illustrates how the apostolic Church seeks to maintain intact the structure of the Twelve, foundational to its identity.

sens: Combine distinct elements to form a homogeneous whole
Adapt or organize parts to create balance
Unite or agree with something or someone
G4786.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a physical mixture: combining different substances to make one. In 1 Corinthians 12:24, Paul uses this image to describe how God has "arranged" the body of the church, that is, how He has mixed and organized the different members to form a unique and balanced body, giving more honor to the weaker parts.
2. The word evokes the idea of adapting or arranging elements so that they harmonize. It is the art of combining what is disparate to create order and proportion, much like mixing the ingredients of a recipe.
3. In Hebrews 4:2, the word takes on a relational nuance: the word "did not find faith" means it did not meet or unite with the faith of those who heard it. The word and faith should have met and combined, but this did not happen due to a lack of reception.
G4786.origine: The word is composed of the prefix σύν (syn, "together") and κεράννυμι (kerannumi, "to pour or mix"). This root evokes the image of a mixture of liquids, particularly in ancient contexts of wine diluted with water. The word fundamentally describes the action of bringing together what was separated to form a new unity.
G4786.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In 1 Corinthians 12:24, it describes God's work in the body of the church: God has mixed and arranged the different members of the body of Christ so that those who seem the weakest receive more honor. In Hebrews 4:2, it takes on a more abstract meaning: the preached word did not "meet" or "unite with" the faith of the listeners, suggesting a lack of reception or spiritual union. In both cases, the verb emphasizes the idea of a meeting, a gathering, or a harmonization between elements.
G4786.portee: This word teaches that God is not a distant creator, but someone who composes, mixes, and balances the elements of life and the church according to His wisdom. For the believer, this means that every member of the body of Christ, including the weakest or most humble, has received their place and role through a thoughtful arrangement by God. The word also reminds us that the word of God only reaches its full effect when it meets and unites with the faith of the heart.

sens: Move together, agitate
Excite, raise (a crowd, a feeling)
G4787.detail: 1. The word combines the idea of "together" (the prefix syn-) and "to move" (kinéō). It literally designates the action of moving several things together, setting them in motion simultaneously. 2. Figuratively, it means to excite or raise — particularly a crowd. In Acts 6:12, it describes how some stir up agitation among the people against Stephen: they do not persuade him calmly, but stir him, pushing him to react passionately and collectively against the accused. It is to move hearts and minds collectively.
G4787.origine: The word comes from the root kinéō ("to move, to set in motion") preceded by the prefix syn ("with, together"). The basic image is thus one of shared or simultaneous movement. This combination of "together" and "movement" naturally applies to the moral and emotional realm: to stir a crowd is to make it move with one heart.
G4787.emploi: The word appears only once in the New Testament, in Acts 6:12, during the trial of Stephen. It describes the action of his accusers who "stir" the people, creating a collective agitation against him. The context shows manipulation: it is not arguments that persuade, but emotional excitement that raises the crowd. This verb emphasizes the power of collective emotion and how easily a community can be set in motion against someone, especially when local authorities orchestrate this reaction.
G4787.portee: This word reminds the reader of the fragility of reason in the face of collective emotion and the power of manipulation. Even a man filled with the Holy Spirit like Stephen can fall victim to stirred crowds excited by those in authority. It is a warning against our susceptibility to being "stirred" without discernment, and a call to examine what truly agitates us: the truth or the passions of the moment.

sens: Enclose or completely shut in
Hold captive, keep under control
Restrict access to something
Figuratively: submit to an authority or condition
G4788.detail:
1. The most concrete meaning is "to enclose on all sides." In Luke 5:6, the net thrown into the lake is filled with fish to the point of breaking: they are enclosed, caught in the meshes of the net that completely encloses them.
2. "Hold captive" or "keep under guard." In Galatians 3:23, Paul says that believers were "kept in custody under the law," meaning held captive, watched over by the law like a guard watches over a prisoner, until faith should come.
3. The word also expresses the idea of restriction: something or someone is enclosed in a condition, with no escape. In Romans 11:32, "God has shut up all men in disobedience": all humanity is maintained in this state, surrounded by Him.
4. In a figurative and theological sense, to enclose means "to submit to," "to subject to." In Galatians 3:22, "the Scripture has confined all under sin": everyone is placed under the power of sin, with no way out through the law — except through faith in Jesus Christ.
G4788.origine: The word comes from the prefix συν- (sun-, "with") and the verb κλείω (kleiō, "to close"). Συγκλείω thus retains the image of complete closure, locking on all sides, reinforced by the prefix "together." This formation expresses the idea of total enclosure, without fissure. The Greek Old Testament uses it to translate סגר (sagar), which also means "to close, to enclose."
G4788.emploi: The word appears four times in the New Testament, always in Paul or in his narratives (Luke, who uses it once). Its initial use in Luke 5:6 is literal: the net is overflowing with fish, it is "thrown" meaning filled and closed. In Paul, the word becomes deeply theological. In Romans 11:32 and Galatians 3:22-23, it describes the human condition under sin and under the law: humanity is "enclosed," subjected to these powers. The law offers no escape (Galatians 3:23); only faith in Christ frees from this enclosure. The word emphasizes the universality of the condition ("all men," "all") and the absence of means to escape by one's own strength.
G4788.portee: This word invites the reader to understand the gravity of the human situation without Christ. We are "enclosed" — prisoners of sin, kept by the law, with no way out by our own hands. But this enclosure, far from being the last word, prepares for grace: God encloses us this way to lead us to faith in Jesus Christ, who alone can free us. The word says that the law is not a definitive prison, but a step toward freedom in Christ.

sens: one who inherits with another or others of the same property
one who shares with others a common promise or blessing
one who receives a common grace
G4789.detail:
1. A co-heir is someone who receives an inheritance at the same time as another or others. It's like when several children share together the house or belongings left to them by a parent: they do not receive them alone, but together. In Hebrews 11:9, Isaac and Jacob are co-heirs of the promise: God made the same promise of the land to all three of them.
2. In the Christian faith, this word refers to one who shares with others a divine blessing or promise. In Romans 8:17, believers are co-heirs with Christ: like children who receive the paternal inheritance together, Christians receive together with Jesus what God promises — but on the condition of suffering with Him.
3. The word also applies to one who receives a common grace with others. In Ephesians 3:6, Paul teaches that the Gentiles who believe become co-heirs with the Jews: all together, without distinction, they inherit the same promise in Jesus Christ. In 1 Peter 3:7, the woman must be honored as one who will inherit with her husband the grace of life.
G4789.origine: The Greek word is composed of two elements: "syn" which means "with" (found in words like "synagogue," assembly) and "klēronomos," one who inherits. In the Bible, inheritance is never just a material possession: it is primarily the possession that God promises to His people. The compound emphasizes that several share together in this divine promise.
G4789.emploi: This word appears 4 times in the New Testament, always to express a shared spiritual inheritance. In Romans 8:17, it is the heart of the Gospel: believers are declared children of God, thus heirs of His promises, and even more, co-heirs with Christ Himself. In Ephesians 3:6, Paul uses it to show the "mystery": that the Gentiles are no longer strangers but citizens of the people of God, heirs with the Jews. In Hebrews 11:9 and 1 Peter 3:7, the word includes one who shares the same promise or grace. It is always a term that unites, that abolishes boundaries.
G4789.portee: This word liberates the one who reads it: you do not inherit alone the promise of God, you share it with all believers, including those you did not expect to meet in the people of God. It is a word of dignity for all — Gentiles with Jews, women with husbands — and an invitation to recognize in each one a brother or sister in the inheritance. It also reminds that this inheritance is not without cost: it is received by suffering with Christ, but it is together that it is received.

sens: to share a common thing with someone
to associate with an action or situation
to stand in solidarity with someone in their trials
to be complicit in a fault or sin
G4790.detail:
1. To take part in means to share an action, experience, or reality with others (Philippians 4:14). It is to be involved together in something that unites us.
2. The word describes the act of associating with a behavior or a set of actions, for example, with the "unfruitful works of darkness" (Ephesians 5:11) — it is to participate in what others do, to be engaged in their actions.
3. To take part in someone's distress means to stand in solidarity with them in their misfortune, to support them by sharing their burden (Philippians 4:14).
4. The word can also mean to be complicit in a fault, to share the responsibility of a sin by not separating from it (Revelation 18:4), in the sense that continuing to participate equates to approval.
G4790.origine: The Greek word combines sun- ("with") and koinōneō ("to have in common, to share"), which itself comes from koinós ("common"). The basic image is that of communion: being together in a shared reality. The preposition "with" (sun-) reinforces the idea of mutual association or involvement.
G4790.emploi: The verb appears three times in the New Testament, always with a sense of participation or solidarity. In Ephesians 5:11, it is about refusing to participate in evil acts. In Philippians 4:14, the Philippians took part in Paul's distress by supporting him, which is commended. In Revelation 18:4, it warns the people not to participate in the sins of Babylon and thus in its judgment. The meaning varies slightly: condemnation of participation in evil, approval of participation in a brother's suffering, and warning against unintentional complicity.
G4790.portee: This word teaches the believer to be attentive to what they associate with: not to participate in evil acts, even if they seem ordinary or hidden (Ephesians 5:11), while being supportive of their brothers in trial (Philippians 4:14). It reminds us that our associations and participations engage us morally and spiritually; remaining faithful to Christ requires choosing with whom and to what we unite.

sens: one who shares something with others
one who has a share in a good or grace
one who is associated with a suffering or trial
G4791.detail:
1. The word designates one who shares something with others, who is associated with it. In Romans 11:17, Paul tells the Gentile believer that he has become a "participant" of the root and fatness of the olive tree, meaning he now enjoys the same blessings as the natural branches of Israel.
2. More broadly, it refers to one who has a share in a common good or grace. In Philippians 1:7, believers "participate" in the grace that belongs to Paul, the grace of Christ that supports and strengthens in trial.
3. The word is also used for one who is associated with a suffering, a tribulation, a trial. In Revelation 1:9, John tells the churches that he is their brother and that he has "part" with them in the tribulation and kingdom of Jesus: he goes through the same persecutions, but with the same hope.
G4791.origine: The word is composed of συν ("with") and κοινωνός, which comes from κοινός ("common"). The basic image is that of sharing, of what is common to several. The root κοινός evokes what belongs to all, what is shared. Thus, συγκοινωνός naturally designates one who participates in a communion, in a common share with others.
G4791.emploi: The word appears only four times in the New Testament. Paul uses it to speak of those who enjoy together a common spiritual blessing (Romans 11:17; 1 Corinthians 9:23; Philippians 1:7) or a common trial (Revelation 1:9). The context shows that participation can be that of a good (grace, the root of the olive tree), of a goal (the Gospel), or of a suffering (the tribulation). It is a word that emphasizes the union and solidarity among believers, or between the believer and Christ in His passion.
G4791.portee: This word enriches the understanding of what it means to be a Christian: not only to receive individual salvation, but to become a participant in a community, to share the promises, grace, and also the sufferings of Christ and His people. It reminds the believer that they are never alone in their faith, that they are connected to others through a real and deep communion.

sens: To receive a body for burial
To pay last respects to a deceased person
To fulfill a duty of piety towards the deceased
G4792.detail:
1. The verb συγκομίζω literally means "to gather together": it is to collect the remains of a deceased person to prepare them for burial. The prefix "sun-" (together) and the root "komiz-" (to transport, to bring) create a very concrete image: one goes to fetch the body and carries it to bury it.

2. In Jewish and Greco-Roman practice, burying the dead is not a simple technical act: it is to fulfill a fundamental religious and familial duty. In Acts 8:2, devout men "buried" Stephen after his martyrdom, an act that expresses both respect for the deceased and faith in the resurrection. This act of receiving the body and committing it to the earth represents an act of love and dignity.

3. The term can also express a form of communal duty: it is never trivial or impersonal, but always marked by piety. Burial shows how the living honor the dead and confess their faith, even in difficult circumstances like the martyrdom of Stephen.
G4792.origine: The Greek word συγκομίζω is composed of the prefix συν- (syn-, "with, together") and κομίζω (komizō, "to transport, to bring, to carry back"). This root expresses the idea of taking care of something by bringing it from one place to another. The composition "together + to transport" creates the image of gathering the remains and carrying them. In Hebrew, the verb עָלָה (ʿālāh, "to go up") can express the action of lifting a body for burial, particularly in passages of the Tanakh translated by this Greek verb in ancient Greek.
G4792.emploi: The verb συγκομίζω is attested only once in the New Testament, in Acts 8:2. It appears in the passive: "Devout men buried Stephen." This choice of word is not trivial: after the brutal martyrdom of the deacon, the Christian community of Jerusalem performs this act of piety to honor his memory and affirm their solidarity with him. In Greek and Jewish tradition, this term also refers to the fulfillment of a sacred duty. The context of martyrdom emphasizes that even in the face of persecution, believers maintain respect for the dead and the dignity of the deceased.
G4792.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reminds us that burial is much more than a formality: it is an act of faith and charity towards one who has given his life for Christ. It also shows that the early Christian community, even when persecuted, upheld its values of respect and compassion. It is a lesson on how to bear witness: not only through the preaching of the resurrection but also through concrete acts of dignity and piety towards the dead.

sens: To assemble together, to combine elements
To set side by side two or more things to examine their similarities and differences
To interpret or explain the meaning of something
G4793.detail:
1. The primary meaning of the word is very concrete: to gather, to assemble several things together. This is indeed the meaning found in 1 Corinthians 2:13, where Paul speaks of "using spiritual language for spiritual things" — that is, matching words to the realities being stated.
2. From this comes the more common meaning: to set face to face, to compare. When we "compare" two realities, we place them side by side for examination. This is exactly what Paul refuses to do in 2 Corinthians 10:12: he does not want to "compare himself" to those who boast, nor measure himself by their standards.
3. A third meaning, especially in the Old Testament, is to interpret: to give meaning to something obscure, as one interprets a dream. This meaning relies on the image of "bringing together" or "putting together" elements to extract hidden meaning.
G4793.origine: The word is formed from the prefix "syn-" (together, with) and the verb "krinō" (to separate, to judge, to criticize). The basic idea is therefore "to separate together" or "to set in relation": one brings two things closer to distinguish, examine, or judge them. In classical Greek and among later authors, the word has specialized in the sense of "to compare." In the Greek Old Testament, it mainly translates the Hebrew verb "patar" (to interpret, to explain), hence the sense of interpretation.
G4793.emploi: The word appears only twice in the New Testament. In 1 Corinthians 2:13, Paul speaks of "assembling" or "matching" spiritual language with spiritual realities — the idea that the word must fit what it speaks about. In 2 Corinthians 10:12, the same apostle categorically refuses to "compare himself" to his opponents or to "measure" himself against them: he rejects this parallel as vain and absurd. In both cases, the word carries the idea of juxtaposition or relation for examination or appreciation.
G4793.portee: This word invites us to seek harmony between word and truth: our words must correspond to the reality we speak of. It also reminds us of the danger of comparing ourselves to others or measuring ourselves by their standards — a constant temptation that distracts us from keeping our eyes fixed on Christ. Comparison diverts us from our personal path with God.

sens: To be bent, leaning forward
To be unable to straighten up, physically or morally
G4794.detail:
1. The verb describes the action of bending or leaning forward. It is a movement of the body that flexes. In Luke 13:11, a woman possessed by a spirit was bent for eighteen years: her body was permanently bent forward.

2. Beyond the simple movement, the word primarily expresses the state of one who can no longer straighten up, who is as if crushed or overwhelmed by a force beyond them. This bending is not a voluntary gesture, but the result of oppression, illness, or spiritual possession. The word thus paints the helplessness and humiliation of the afflicted person.
G4794.origine: The verb is composed of two parts: "syn" (together, with) and "kyptô" (to bend, to curve). This composition suggests a complete, total bending. The word belongs to the family of verbs that describe a flexion of the body. In Hebrew, a similar type of image is used to speak of someone who is burdened or oppressed.
G4794.emploi: The verb appears only once in the New Testament, in Luke 13:11. Jesus encounters a woman bent for eighteen years due to a spirit. This unique usage shows the word in the context of physical suffering and spiritual oppression. The miracle of Jesus, who straightens her up, takes on full significance: he not only frees her from the evil that oppresses her but also restores her dignity and bodily integrity.
G4794.portee: This scene reminds us that physical suffering, even seemingly ordinary, can hide a profound spiritual reality. It also shows us that Jesus does not merely speak: he concretely liberates those who are crushed by evil. For us, this account invites us to recognize forms of spiritual oppression around us and to believe in Jesus' power to lift up and restore.

sens: Fortuitous encounter, unexpected occurrence of an event without apparent cause
Coincidence of events that seem due to fate rather than intention
G4795.detail:
1. Chance is an encounter or event that happens without being anticipated or sought. In Luke 10:31, the priest who "by chance" goes down the same road as the wounded man did not know he would cross paths with him: the encounter seems purely accidental, occurring by the luck of the moment.
2. The word also evokes the idea that certain things happen without an explainable reason, purely by coincidence. But for a Christian, what the world calls "chance" reminds us that God governs all things, even what seems fortuitous in our eyes.
G4795.origine: The Greek word comes from the verb "happening" (to occur, to happen). It is formed with the prefix "syn-" (together) and "kyros" (the opportune occasion), hence the idea of events that happen "together" without a plan. It is a rare word in the New Testament but more common in late Greek. It translates in Ezekiel 1:27 the Hebrew word "mikreh" which literally means "that which falls" or "that which happens by chance."
G4795.emploi: The word appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in Luke 10:31, in the parable of the Good Samaritan. There, Jesus uses it to describe how a priest happens to pass by the road where a wounded man lies. The term emphasizes the unpredictable aspect of the encounter from a human perspective: the priest does not know he will see him. Yet, this "coincidence" introduces Jesus' teaching on the neighbor and mercy, showing that God can use what seems like chance to fulfill His purposes.
G4795.portee: This word invites reflection on the difference between human perspective and that of God. What we call chance or misfortune is known and governed by God. This does not diminish our responsibility to act with charity when an opportunity arises, as the Samaritan did: it is precisely in these seemingly fortuitous encounters that God places us face to face with our duties.

sens: share in someone else's joy
participate together in joy
express joyful sympathy
G4796.detail:
1. To share in someone else's joy: the word denotes being happy with someone else, rejoicing together over a happy event. This is what the neighbors of Elizabeth do when they learn of the mercy the Lord has shown her: they "rejoiced with her" (Luke 1:58).
2. To participate together in joy: it is also inviting others to share in one's own joy, like the shepherd who calls his friends and neighbors saying, "Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost sheep" (Luke 15:6). Joy is not isolated; it becomes communal.
3. To express joyful sympathy: in the Church, it is the ability to rejoice with those who are honored or who do good. The Apostle Paul teaches that if one member is honored, "all the members rejoice with him" (1 Corinthians 12:26), and love "rejoices in the truth" (1 Corinthians 13:6).
G4796.origine: The Greek word is composed of the prefix "syn" (with) and the verb "chairô" (to rejoice, to be glad). The image is that of joy being shared, uniting several people. This compound illustrates the biblical theme of communion in emotions and experiences: one does not rejoice alone, but with others.
G4796.emploi: The verb appears about 7 times in the New Testament, primarily in Luke and Paul. In Luke, it describes the reaction of those close to divine mercies manifested (Luke 1:58; 15:6, 9): people rejoice together when God acts. In Paul, the word takes on a broader ecclesial dimension: in 1 Corinthians 12:26, it expresses the unity of the body of Christ where joy is shared among all members; in 1 Corinthians 13:6, it characterizes love that rejoices in good and truth; in Philippians 2:17-18, it expresses the communion of joy between the apostle and the believers.
G4796.portee: This word reminds us that Christian joy should not remain isolated: it flourishes when shared. Doing good, receiving mercy, or advancing in truth are not fully joyful unless others rejoice with us. It is a call to fraternal communion and empathy: rejoicing with those who are happy is as important as weeping with those who weep. This virtue builds the unity of the body of Christ.

sens: Mix together, blur
Disturb the mind, confuse someone
Throw into disorder, confusion
Stir up a crowd, create agitation
G4797.detail:
1. The primary meaning is physical: to mix or blur together. When the crowd in Acts 2:6 hears each speaking in their own language, they are "confounded" because all these sounds are jumbled and no one understands what is happening.

2. On an intellectual and moral level, the verb means to confuse someone, to put them in difficulty by the force of argumentation. Saul in Damascus "confounded" the Jews, meaning he silenced them by logically demonstrating that Jesus is the Christ (Acts 9:22).

3. The word also describes the state of disorder and confusion that reigns in an assembly. In Ephesus, "disorder" seizes the crowd of spectators at the theater, each shouting in their own way without knowing why (Acts 19:32).

4. Finally, it means to stir up a crowd to revolt, to create tumult. The Jews from Asia "stir up" the whole crowd against Paul (Acts 21:27), causing a general "confusion" in Jerusalem (Acts 21:31).
G4797.origine: The word comes from the prefix "syn" (together) and the verb "chéō" (to pour, to spread). The basic image is that of pouring together, mixing liquids. This is why the word acquires the meaning of blurring, mixing confusingly, both literally and figuratively. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew "bâlal" (to mix) and "râgaz" (to stir, to tremble), showing how physical disorder and emotional agitation are linked.
G4797.emploi: This verb appears only in the Acts of the Apostles, always in a context of trouble or agitation. In Acts 2:6, the crowd is confounded by mutual incomprehension. In Acts 9:22, Saul confounds his intellectual opponents. In Acts 19:32 and 21:31, the word denotes physical and social tumult: stirred-up crowds, public disorder, urban confusion. The verb thus paints the opposition faced by the apostles: misunderstanding, refutation in debate, or collective violence. In all cases, a balance or clarity is disturbed.
G4797.portee: This word shows us how apostolic preaching causes trouble: it disturbs minds, undermines established certainties, and provokes reactions. For the Christian reader, it reminds us that the word of God does not leave one indifferent — it confounds the wise (in the sense of silencing them with truth) and it provokes opposition. It is both the effectiveness of the message and the cost of testimony.

sens: To use together, to share in common
To have relationships, exchanges with someone
To associate with someone regularly
G4798.detail:
1. The word primarily refers to the idea of using something together with others, of sharing. It is the basic image of the compound verb: "with" and "to use."

2. Applied to people, this means to have social relationships, to maintain ties of friendship or commerce with someone. In John 4:9, Jesus asks a Samaritan woman for a drink, which scandalizes: Jews had no relationships with Samaritans, meaning they refused ordinary exchanges, even civil ones, with them. The word thus describes the refusal to live together on a social level.

3. In common usage, the verb can refer to the simple act of associating with someone, talking to them, spending time with them — something everyone naturally does with their fellow citizens, except when a religious or cultural barrier prohibits it.
G4798.origine: The word is composed of the prefix "with" (syn-) and the verb "to use, to employ, to treat" (chraomai). This composition suggests the idea of shared use, of common practice. The same root is found in other Greek words that express use or exchange. In Hebrew, the idea of "relationships" with someone can be expressed by verbs indicating closeness or sharing (such as "to dwell together"), although this Greek verb is only attested in John 4.
G4798.emploi: This verb appears only once in the New Testament, in John 4:9. Jesus, sitting at Jacob's well, asks a Samaritan woman for a drink. She expresses her astonishment: not only is he a man speaking alone with a woman (which was contrary to customs), but he is Jewish, and Jews refused any relationship with Samaritans. This refusal was deep-rooted: it stemmed from the ancient schism between northern and southern Israel and had crystallized into mutual hostility. The text of John uses this word to show that Jesus breaks a religious barrier by simply asking for a drink. The verb summarizes the entire issue of the narrative: the social and religious exclusion that Jesus refuses to accept.
G4798.portee: This passage reveals that religious prejudices can lead us to refuse even ordinary, basic relationships with those we consider different or enemies. By asking this woman for a drink, Jesus invites us to break these barriers and recognize our common humanity. For a Christian, this gesture of the Savior calls for humility: no cultural or religious difference should prevent us from showing courtesy, respect, and openness to others. It is the beginning of a heart transformation.

sens: Disorder, agitation, general trouble among a crowd
State of chaos where people rush in disarray
Popular tumult, riot
G4799.detail:
1. Confusion is primarily a complete disorder, a trouble that seizes a crowd. It is the image of several people losing their footing together and colliding in chaos. In Ephesus, when Demetrius incites a disturbance against Paul, the whole city falls into confusion: people rush to the theater without order or reflection (Acts 19:29).
2. It is also the collective emotional tumult, when panic or anger overwhelms a multitude and drives them to thoughtless action. The Old Testament uses a Hebrew word to denote this chaos, evoking trouble and riot, notably during the construction of Babel where languages are confused and create complete disorder.
G4799.origine: The word comes from the Greek verb meaning "to mix, to pour together, to disturb." The starting image is that of a confused mixture, where things and people blur instead of being distinct and ordered. In the Greek Old Testament, this word translates the Hebrew that describes trouble, chaotic noise, and disorder. The root always suggests this idea of things intertwining and getting lost.
G4799.emploi: This word appears only once in the Greek New Testament, in Acts 19:29, during the riot in Ephesus provoked by the idol merchants of Artemis threatened by Paul's preaching. It is therefore a rare term, reserved to depict a moment of chaotic urban tumult. The ancient use of the word in the Septuagint (Greek translation of the Old Testament) connects it to accounts of collective troubles like Babel, showing that the idea of confusion always implies a rupture of order.
G4799.portee: This word helps us grasp how the Christian message sometimes provokes trouble in society, and how the crowd can become unruly without reflection. It reminds us that in the face of resistance and tumult, Christians are called to clarity of heart, while a godless world can fall into chaos and confusion.
